components/buttons.title: Buttons
components/buttons.text: Buttons Every button returns true on the frame it is clicked : a press and a release over it. A pressed button keeps the pointer until the release, even if it strays; letting go outside is no click. The pointer turns into a hand over it. A screen reader reads it as "label, button" and can press it. Button and PrimaryButton Button for ordinary actions, PrimaryButton for the one main action of a place: Save in a form, Remove in a sheet that asks first. Put the primary last on the right. context.Label("Save the changes to North Point?") context.Row(func() { context.Spacer() if context.Button("Cancel") { // close without saving } if context.PrimaryButton("Save") { // one primary action per place saved++ } }) Save the changes? with Cancel and a blue Save When the words change but it is the same button (Switch on, Switch off), keep its id with ## : context.PrimaryButton(label + "##switch") . IconButton and PrimaryIconButton An icon before the words, or an icon alone (an empty label makes it square). Use icons alone only for actions everyone knows (zoom, close, undo), and give them a tooltip. context.Row(func() { if context.IconButton("minus", "") { // square: an icon alone zoom-- } context.Label(fmt.Sprintf("Zoom %d", zoom)) if context.IconButton("plus", "") { zoom++ } context.Spacer() context.IconButton("download", "Export") // an icon before the words context.PrimaryIconButton("plus", "New lighthouse") }) − Zoom 1 + on the left, Export and a blue New lighthouse on the right FlatButton and FlatIconButton No fill or border until the pointer is over them: menu bars, toolbars, and actions inside a row that should not shout. context.Frame(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.PadXY(8, 4), Gap: 2, AlignY: ui.Center}, ui.Look{Fill: context.Theme.Surface, Radius: 6}, func() { context.FlatIconButton("undo-2", "") context.FlatIconButton("redo-2", "") context.Separator() context.FlatButton("File") context.FlatButton("Edit") context.FlatIconButton("eye", "View") }) A toolbar with undo, redo, File, Edit and View Selectable An item that shows whether it is chosen, and returns true when clicked. In a row it fits its content (a group of tools); in a column it takes the whole width (a side list). It does not change anything itself: your variable decides which one is chosen. context.Row(func() { // in a row: a group of tools, fitted for _, name := range []string{"move", "pencil", "eraser"} { if context.Selectable(name, "", tool == name) { tool = name } } }) context.Column(func() { // in a column: a side list, full width for index, name := range []string{"Inbox", "Lighthouses", "Keepers"} { if context.Selectable("folder", name, place == index) { place = index } } }) Three tool icons, the first chosen; a list of three folders, Inbox chosen A screen reader reads it as selected or not. Chip and RemovableChip Small rounded labels: a state, a filter, a tag. Chip returns true when clicked; RemovableChip has a small × and returns clicked, removed apart. ui.ChipLook{Fill, Ink} gives their colours (zero: the theme's quiet ones). To let a row of chips flow onto more lines, put them in a box with Wrap: true and a width that does not follow its content. context.Row(func() { // filters: click to choose one for _, state := range []string{"All", "Lit", "Dark"} { look := ui.ChipLook{} if filter == state { look = ui.ChipLook{Fill: context.Theme.PrimaryTint, Ink: context.Theme.Primary} } if context.Chip("", state, look) { filter = state } } }) context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Wrap: true, Gap: 6}, func() { // tags: remove them for index := 0; index < len(tags); index++ { if _, removed := context.RemovableChip("tag", tags[index], ui.ChipLook{}); removed { tags = append(tags[:index], tags[index+1:]...) index-- } } }) context.Chip("circle-alert", "Needs repair", ui.ChipLook{Fill: draw2d.MustHex("#fdecea"), Ink: draw2d.MustHex("#b3261e")}) Three filter chips, four tags with ×, a red Needs repair chip Clickable Any box that reacts to the pointer, with its own look while left alone, hovered and pressed. It is what Go UI's own buttons are made of, and the way to make a card, a row or a tile clickable as a whole. Buttons inside it keep their own clicks. theme := context.Theme cards := []struct{ icon, title, text string }{ {"lighthouse", "Lighthouse", "A tower with a light"}, {"anchor", "Harbour", "Berths and a mole"}, } context.Row(func() { for index, card := range cards { looks := ui.Looks{ Normal: ui.Look{Fill: theme.Surface, Border: theme.Line, BorderWidth: 1, Radius: 8}, Hovered: ui.Look{Fill: theme.Surface, Border: theme.Primary, BorderWidth: 1, Radius: 8}, Pressed: ui.Look{Fill: theme.PrimaryTint, Border: theme.Primary, BorderWidth: 1, Radius: 8}, } if index == chosen { looks.Normal = looks.Pressed } layout := ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Share(1), Padding: ui.Pad(12), Gap: 4} if context.Clickable(card.title, layout, looks, func() { context.Icon(card.icon) context.Heading(card.title) context.Caption(card.text) }) { chosen = index } } }) Two cards, Lighthouse chosen with a blue border, Harbour beside it A screen reader reads the texts inside it as a button. If it is something else (a switch, a tab), say so after it with context.Describe(ui.Description{Role: …}) . LongPressed Tells whether the control added just before it was held : a finger still on it for half a second, or the right mouse button. A touch that became a long press is no click. Use it for a second action on the same thing: choosing rows, a context menu. if context.Selectable("file", name, chosen[name]) { open(name) } if context.LongPressed() { chosen[name] = true // start choosing several } ← Text, icons and pictures · Choices →

components/choices.title: Choices
components/choices.text: Choices Controls that edit a value of yours. Each takes a pointer to it, writes the new value as the person acts, and returns true on the frame it changed: read your variable everywhere else, and use the true only for what should happen once (a note, saving). Checkbox and Toggle Both edit a bool . A checkbox is a fact about what is being edited, often one of several in a form, applied with the form. A toggle (a switch on the right of its label) is a setting that takes effect at once. context.Checkbox("Has a foghorn", &foghorn) // a fact about the thing being edited context.Separator() context.Toggle("Notify me when a lamp fails", &notify) // a setting that takes effect at once context.Toggle("Light at dusk on its own", &autoLight) A ticked checkbox, a line, and two settings rows with switches Clicking the label flips it too. A screen reader says "ticked" or "on". Slider and SliderStep A value between two ends, dragged. Click the track to jump, drag the knob, hold Shift to move ten times slower. SliderStep keeps whole steps. A slider shows no number: put one beside it when the exact value matters, or use a number field. context.Row(func() { context.Icon("volume-1") context.Slider("volume", &volume, 0, 1) // any value: a volume, an opacity context.Icon("volume-2") }) context.Row(func() { context.Label("Period") context.SliderStep("period", &period, 1, 20, 1) // whole seconds only context.Caption(fmt.Sprintf("%.0f s", period)) }) A volume slider between two speaker icons, and a period slider with 5 s beside it A screen reader reads its range and moves it a step at a time. NumberField A number with − and + on its sides, for exact values. Click − or +, drag the number sideways (a step every 4 pixels), or click it and type (a point or a comma for decimals; Enter keeps it, Escape does not). The format ( fmt style) shows the unit. context.Row(func() { context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Fixed(90)}, func() { context.Label("Range") }) context.NumberField("range", &rangeNM, 1, 30, 1, "%.0f nm") }) context.Row(func() { context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Fixed(90)}, func() { context.Label("Height") }) context.NumberField("height", &height, 0, 200, 0.5, "%.1f m") }) Range 18 nm and Height 32.5 m, each with − and + Select One choice of a list, shown in a field; clicking opens the list over everything, under the field or above it when there is no room. Choose with a click, or the arrows and Enter; Escape or a click elsewhere closes it. While open it holds the keyboard. colours := []string{"White", "Red", "Green", "Amber"} context.Row(func() { context.Label("Light colour") if context.Select("colour", &colour, colours) { context.Toast("Colour set to "+colours[colour], false) } }) Light colour: Red, in a field with a chevron For two to four short options always in sight, use Tabs instead. Tabs A segmented row, the chosen segment raised. It only chooses: show what belongs to the tab with an if or a switch , like any other content. context.Tabs("view", &tab, "General", "Light", "History") switch tab { case 0: context.Label("North Point, on the northern cliffs.") case 1: context.Label("White, every five seconds.") case 2: context.Label("Built a long time ago.") } Tabs General, Light and History, General chosen, and its text ListBox A scrolling list of selectable items, for a choice among more options than a select should hold and that the person should see at once. keepers := []string{"First keeper", "Second keeper", "Relief keeper", "Boatman", "Cook", "Signal officer"} context.Label("Who is on duty?") context.ListBox("keepers", ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Fixed(130)}, keepers, &keeper) Who is on duty? and a list of keepers with Relief keeper chosen ← Buttons · Text fields →

components/components.title: Components
components/components.text: Components Every Go UI control, one by one: what it is for, concrete cases with their code, how it behaves with the mouse, the keyboard, a finger and a screen reader, and its options. Each case is a real program's code; the pictures are captures of it. All the cases assume the usual frame: context is the *ui.Context your build function gets ( window.Run ) or that you call Begin and End on. State such as tab or foghorn is a variable of your program that lives between frames. Page Components Text, icons and pictures Heading , Label , Caption , Text , Icon , IconSized , Image , Tooltip Buttons Button , PrimaryButton , IconButton , PrimaryIconButton , FlatButton , FlatIconButton , Selectable , Chip , RemovableChip , Clickable , LongPressed Choices Checkbox , Toggle , Slider , SliderStep , NumberField , Select , Tabs , ListBox Text fields TextField , TextFieldWith , focus, validation, search Containers Box , Frame , Row , Column , Grid , Spacer , Separator , ScrollArea , Fold , Paint , SwipeBox Lists and tables List , Table Layers Panel , PanelWith , Sheet , Modal , Overlay , Popover , MenuButton , MenuItem , Toast Dragging and resizing DragSource , DropTarget , Dragging , DroppedOnScreen , Resizable A design system's look The theme's design tokens: buttons, the chosen item, line heights, check boxes, focus and press Who has the keyboard KeyboardNavigation , TakeKeyboard , ReleaseKeyboard , HasKeyboard , LessMotion : Tab, Enter and Space beside a game or a 3D view Rules every control follows A control is a call. It is drawn in the frame it is called in, and gone in the frame it is not. Show it with an if ; repeat it with a for . It answers what happened in this frame. Buttons return true on the frame they are clicked; controls that edit a value take a pointer to it and return true on the frame they change it. It is told apart by its label and its scopes (its id ). In a loop, open a scope per item with context.Push(name) … context.Pop() . Text after ## is part of the id but not shown. Colours and sizes come from context.Theme . Change a token and every control follows. The pointer works from the last frame's layout , so a control reacts where it was drawn. ← Documentation

components/containers.title: Containers
components/containers.text: Containers Boxes arrange what is inside them. Their ui.Layout gives a direction, sizes ( Fit , Grow , Share , Fixed , Percent ), padding, a gap and alignment; the guide explains how sizes are worked out. Box and Frame Box only arranges. Frame also paints, with a ui.Look : fill, border, corner radius, a shadow for things that float, and a clip. Cards side by side with Share(1) come out the same width. theme := context.Theme card := ui.Look{Fill: theme.Surface, Border: theme.Line, BorderWidth: 1, Radius: 8, Shadow: true} context.Row(func() { for _, figure := range [][2]string{{"Lighthouses", "12"}, {"Lit", "9"}, {"Keepers", "4"}} { context.Frame(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Share(1), Padding: ui.Pad(12), Gap: 4}, card, func() { context.Caption(figure[0]) context.Text(figure[1], ui.TextStyle{Size: 24, Weight: draw2d.Bold}) }) } }) Three cards with Lighthouses 12, Lit 9, Keepers 4 Row, Column, Spacer, Separator Row is a full-width horizontal box with the theme's gap, its children centred vertically; Column the same, vertical. Spacer takes the free space and pushes what follows to the far end (a button on the right of a bar). Separator is a thin line across its row or column. context.Row(func() { context.Heading("North Point") context.Spacer() context.Button("Edit") }) context.Separator() Grid Rows of equal cells, left to right and then down: Grid(columns, content) , or any box with Layout.Columns . context.Grid(4, func() { for _, icon := range []string{"lighthouse", "anchor", "ship", "waves", "sun", "moon", "cloud", "wind"} { context.Frame(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(12), AlignX: ui.Center}, ui.Look{Fill: context.Theme.Sunken, Radius: 6}, func() { context.Icon(icon) }) } }) Two rows of four tiles, each with an icon ScrollArea Content taller than its box scrolls: the wheel or a trackpad over it, the thin bar on its right, or a finger, which glides on when let go. Give it a height that does not follow its content ( Fixed , or Grow in a column), or it simply grows. context.ScrollArea("log", ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Fixed(120), Gap: 4}, func() { for day := 1; day <= 30; day++ { context.Label(fmt.Sprintf("Day %d: lamp lit at dusk", day)) } }) Six lines of a thirty-day log, with a scroll bar ScrollOffset(name) says how far it is scrolled (a bar that shrinks over it); ScrollPull(name) measures a pull past its top (a list that refreshes). Fold A box that opens to its content's height and closes to nothing, with motion: the answer under a question, more under a row. While closed, its content is not built at all. if context.FlatIconButton("chevron-down", "When is the lamp lit?") { open = !open } context.Fold("answer", open, 200*time.Millisecond, ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.PadXY(12, 4)}, func() { context.Label("From sunset to sunrise, and in fog.") }) When is the lamp lit? with its answer open under it Paint A box laid out like any other, then handed to your function with its final rectangle and a draw2d.List : for shapes no control draws (a chart, a gauge, a timeline). readings := []float32{0.2, 0.5, 0.4, 0.8, 0.6, 0.9, 0.7} primary := context.Theme.Primary context.Paint(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Fixed(80)}, func(area draw2d.Rectangle, drawing *draw2d.List) { barWidth := area.Width / float32(len(readings)) for index, reading := range readings { height := area.Height * reading bar := draw2d.Rectangle{X: area.X + float32(index)*barWidth + 4, Y: area.Bottom() - height, Width: barWidth - 8, Height: height} drawing.Rectangle(bar, 3, primary, draw2d.Transparent, 0) } }) context.Caption("Hours of fog, this week") Seven bars of different heights and Hours of fog, this week SwipeBox A box a finger drags along one axis: pages, cards in a row, a row swiped away. Your content gets a ui.Swipe (the offset, the speed, whether it is held or just let go) and places itself by it. context.SwipeBox("pages", ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Fixed(200)}, ui.Horizontal, func(swipe ui.Swipe) { if swipe.Released && swipe.Offset < -swipe.Area.Width/3 { page++ // let go past a third of the way: the next page } … }) It takes a finger only along its own axis, so a list inside pages still scrolls up and down. ← Text fields · Lists and tables →

components/design-systems.title: A design system's look

sections.text: A design system that uses them

components/design-systems.text: A design system's look A design system is more than a palette: it decides how a chosen item looks, whether the main button stands out, how tall a line of text is. go-ui's theme has a token for each of those, so a design system can dress every control without the program drawing any of them by hand. You don't need any of this to use go-ui: left at zero, these tokens keep go-ui's own look. The shortest way Start from a theme of go-ui's, then set what your design system asks for: theme := ui.LightTheme() theme.Primary, theme.OnPrimary = draw2d.MustHex("#2f6f8f"), draw2d.MustHex("#ffffff") theme.ButtonRadius, theme.ButtonPadding, theme.ButtonWeight = 10, 18, draw2d.Bold theme.PrimaryEdge, theme.EdgeWidth = draw2d.MustHex("#214e64"), 2 // the main button stands on a block theme.Chosen, theme.ChosenInk = theme.Sunken, theme.Ink // what is chosen is brighter, not coloured theme.LineHeight, theme.HeadingLineHeight = 1.5, 1.2 context.Theme = theme // before the first control of the frame Every button, list and check box of the frame now follows it. The tokens Token What it changes go-ui's own look (when zero) ButtonRadius , ButtonPadding , ButtonGap , ButtonWeight A button's corners, the room on each side of its label, the gap after its icon, its label's weight The controls' corners, 12 pixels a side, 6 of gap PrimaryEdge , EdgeWidth A solid band under the main button, as if it stood on a block; it takes no room, like a shadow No edge FlatHeight , FlatPadding , FlatInk A flat button's height, room and ink at rest A little shorter than the others, in soft ink, for toolbars Chosen , ChosenInk , ChosenWeight How a selected item of a list looks The primary colour's tint ItemPadding , ItemGap , ItemIconInk The room in an item of a list, the gap after its icon, the icon's ink 8 and 8, soft icons LineHeight , HeadingLineHeight A line as tall as its size × this, and the same for text at HeadingSize and above As tall as the letters CheckSize , CheckRadius , CheckBorder , CheckMark , CheckLine , CheckedBorder A check box's side, corners, edge, tick, empty edge and ticked edge go-ui's small box BackdropBlur Blurs what is behind every translucent panel, as frosted glass, by this many pixels Nothing blurred, at no cost FocusWidth The width of the ring around the control Tab reached, lying on its edge; inside a primary button, in OnPrimary 3 pixels FieldFocusEdge A field being typed in lights its own edge in FocusRing instead of a ring around it A ring around the field PressScale How big a held control is drawn (0.97 gives a little); with context.LessMotion set it stays still It keeps its size BackdropBlur frosts a translucent panel that is not inside another one: the rows hovered or chosen inside a frosted panel are translucent too, but blurring again under them would cost a blur for nothing. go-renderer takes one snapshot of the frame per layer, however many panels it has, and blurs it small; its guide to the overlay says what that costs. Two rules keep old themes looking the same: A zero size, or an invisible colour, means go-ui's own look , so a theme made before these tokens existed draws as it always did. The chosen item follows the primary colour while Chosen and ChosenInk are left alone, so a theme that only changes Primary and PrimaryTint still marks it with its own tint. A design system that uses them Bubble 4 , akrck02's design system, makes its themes in Go with their contrast tested, and its goui module turns one into a go-ui theme. Its guide shows the same screen in a browser and in go-ui, side by side, in every style and finish. go-ui itself knows nothing of Bubble: any design system can do the same with these tokens. ← Components

components/dragging-and-resizing.title: Dragging and resizing
components/dragging-and-resizing.text: Dragging and resizing DragSource and DropTarget Drag a value of yours ( any ) from one box to another. A press that moves four pixels becomes a drag; less is a click, which DragSource returns, so a chip inside can still be clicked. While dragging, the source's name follows the pointer, the interface holds the mouse and the keyboard, and Escape cancels. A target says which payloads it takes ( accepts ; nil takes any), is highlighted while one is over it, and returns it on the frame it is let go there. With targets inside targets, the innermost takes it. theme := context.Theme context.Caption("Drag a tag onto the lens") context.Row(func() { for _, tag := range []tagName{"Stone", "Painted", "Listed"} { context.DragSource(string(tag), tag, ui.Layout{}, func() { context.Chip("tag", string(tag), ui.ChipLook{}) }) } }) isTag := func(payload any) bool { _, ok := payload.(tagName); return ok } target := ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(12), Gap: 6} payload, dropped := context.DropTarget("lens", target, isTag, func() { context.Frame(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(12), Gap: 6}, ui.Look{Border: theme.Line, BorderWidth: 1, Radius: 8}, func() { context.Label("Lens:") for _, tag := range onPart { context.Chip("", string(tag), ui.ChipLook{Fill: theme.PrimaryTint, Ink: theme.Primary}) } }) }) if dropped { onPart = append(onPart, payload.(tagName)) } Three tags to drag, and the lens's box with Stone on it Onto the scene Let go over the open screen (no panel, painted box or target) and the payload is the program's: DroppedOnScreen() gives it with the pointer's place, to put it in a 3D scene ( viewer.View.PointOnGround ). Dragging() tells about a drag in progress, to preview where it would land. context.End() if drop, dropped := context.DroppedOnScreen(); dropped { placeAt(groundAt(drop.X, drop.Y), drop.Payload) } Resizable A box with a handle on one side: RightSide for a column on the left of the window, LeftSide for one on the right, BottomSide and TopSide for strips. Dragging the handle writes the new size into your variable, between a minimum and a maximum (0 = none); keep the variable and save it if you like. context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Fixed(140)}, func() { column := ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Height: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(8)} context.Resizable("side", ui.RightSide, &width, 120, 320, column, func() { context.Label("Side list") context.Caption("Drag my right edge") }) context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(8)}, func() { context.Label("Content") }) }) A side list with a line on its right edge, and the content beside it ← Layers · Components

components/layers.title: Layers
components/layers.text: Layers What floats over the rest. What is described later in a frame is drawn on top; popups (menus, selects, tooltips) go over everything. Panel and PanelWith A floating card with a title bar: drag the bar to move it, the chevron folds it, pressing it brings it to the front. Its title opens a scope, so controls in two panels never mix. PanelOptions places it ( X , Y ), sizes it, Locked stops it moving, and Dock fills a side of the window. context.PanelWith("Lamp", ui.PanelOptions{X: 16, Y: 16, Width: ui.Fixed(220)}, func() { context.Toggle("Lit", &on) context.Caption("Drag the title to move me") }) context.PanelWith("Tools", ui.PanelOptions{Dock: ui.DockRight, Width: ui.Fixed(160)}, func() { context.Selectable("move", "Move", true) context.Selectable("pencil", "Draw", false) }) A floating Lamp panel with a switch, and a Tools panel docked on the right Panels are for tools over a scene or a canvas. An application's fixed parts (bars, side columns) are better as boxes on the screen ( containers ). Sheet A modal card in the middle of the window, shown with an if for as long as your program wants. Everything behind is dimmed and does not react; Tab goes round the sheet's own fields. It returns true on the frame the person asks to close it: Escape, the × or a click on the backdrop. if context.Button("Remove North Point") { confirming = true } if confirming && context.Sheet("Remove lighthouse", ui.SheetOptions{Width: ui.Fixed(360)}, func() { context.Label("North Point leaves the register.") context.Row(func() { context.Spacer() if context.Button("Keep it") { confirming = false } if context.PrimaryButton("Remove") { confirming = false } }) }) { confirming = false // Escape, the × or a click on the dimmed backdrop } A Remove lighthouse sheet over the dimmed window, with Keep it and Remove Modal Like a sheet, but drawn entirely by you: a welcome card, a dialog of your own, a drawer. Place it with LayerOptions ( AlignX , AlignY , Padding , Width , Height ); Leave lets it go with motion. if open && context.Modal("welcome", ui.LayerOptions{AlignX: ui.Center, AlignY: ui.Center}, func() { context.Frame(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Padding: ui.Pad(24), Gap: 12, Width: ui.Fixed(300), AlignX: ui.Center}, ui.Look{Fill: context.Theme.Surface, Radius: 12, Shadow: true}, func() { context.IconSized("lighthouse", 40, context.Theme.Primary) context.Heading("Welcome to the register") context.Caption("Every lighthouse on the coast, in one place.") if context.PrimaryButton("Start") { open = false } }) }) { open = false } A welcome card with an icon, a title, a line and a Start button over a dimmed window Overlay(name, options, content) is the same without dimming or blocking: a note at the bottom, a floating button. MenuButton and MenuItem A flat button that opens a menu under it. The menu's content is described only while it is open; MenuItem(icon, label, hint) returns true when chosen, and choosing closes it. Arrows and Enter work. The hint (a shortcut's keys) is only shown: handle the shortcut yourself. context.Row(func() { context.MenuButton("plus", "Add", func() { if context.MenuItem("lighthouse", "Lighthouse", "Ctrl+N") { // add one } if context.MenuItem("anchor", "Harbour", "") { // add one } context.Separator() if context.MenuItem("copy", "Copy of the selected one", "Ctrl+D") { // copy } }) }) Popover A box of your own floating under the control added just before it, at least as wide: a small form about one thing, a dropdown of your own. A click outside, Escape or the back gesture closes it ( open becomes false ). context.Row(func() { if context.IconButton("clock", "Light at dusk") { open = !open } context.Popover("hour", &open, ui.Look{Fill: context.Theme.Surface, Border: context.Theme.Line, BorderWidth: 1, Radius: 8, Shadow: true}, func() { context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Padding: ui.Pad(12), Gap: 8, Width: ui.Fixed(220)}, func() { context.Caption("Hour the lamp is lit") context.NumberField("hour", &hour, 0, 23, 1, "%.0f:00") }) }) }) A Light at dusk button with a card under it holding the hour, 20:00 Toast A short note at the bottom for a few seconds. Unlike everything else it is fired once , when something happens, not described at every frame; true as the second argument makes it a warning. if context.Button("Save") || first { context.Toast("North Point was saved", false) // fired once; it fades on its own } if context.Button("Check the lamp") { context.Toast("The lamp did not answer", true) // a warning } ← Lists and tables · Dragging and resizing →

components/lists-and-tables.title: Lists and tables
components/lists-and-tables.text: Lists and tables List A scroll area of rows of the same height that builds only the rows in sight: ten thousand rows cost what twenty do. The row function gets the index; ids inside it are scoped by it, so no Push is needed. const count = 10000 context.List("buoys", ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Fixed(150)}, count, 28, func(index int) { if context.Selectable("circle-dot", fmt.Sprintf("Buoy %d", index+1), index == selected) { selected = index } }) context.Caption(fmt.Sprintf("%d buoys; only the rows in sight are built", count)) Buoy 1 to 5 in a scrolling list, Buoy 4 chosen, and a caption For a few dozen rows of different heights, a ScrollArea with a for is simpler. Table A header that stays while the rows scroll, columns that line up, group captions, a chosen row with a strip of the primary colour. Row(id, selected, cells...) returns true when clicked; cells are text, and text that does not fit ends in "…". type part struct { group, name, code string count int } parts := []part{ {"Lantern", "Lens", "LN-01", 1}, {"Lantern", "Lamp", "LN-02", 2}, {"Lantern", "Clockwork", "LN-03", 1}, {"Tower", "Stairs", "TW-01", 112}, {"Tower", "Windows", "TW-02", 8}, } columns := []ui.Column{ {Title: "Part", Width: ui.Share(1)}, {Title: "Code", Width: ui.Fixed(72)}, {Title: "Count", Width: ui.Fixed(56), Align: ui.End}, // numbers on the right } context.Table("parts", ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Fixed(220)}, columns, func(table *ui.Table) { for index, item := range parts { if index == 0 || item.group != parts[index-1].group { table.Group(item.group) } if table.Row(item.code, index == selected, item.name, item.code, strconv.Itoa(item.count)) { selected = index } } }) A table of parts in two groups, Lantern and Tower, with Lamp chosen ui.Column field Means Title The header's words Width Fixed for narrow columns, Share for the rest: header and rows come out the same Align ui.Start for words, ui.End for numbers Weight draw2d.Mono for a column of codes table.RowWith(id, selected, ui.RowLook{Icon, IconInk, Tile, Indent, Secondary}, cells...) starts the first cell with an icon on a tinted tile, a second quieter line, or an indent for a row that belongs to the one above. Rows and captions out of sight are only counted, so a few thousand rows are fine; give the table a height that does not follow its content. ← Containers · Layers →

components/text.title: Text, icons and pictures
components/text.text: Text, icons and pictures Heading, Label, Caption Three levels of text for nearly everything: a bold title, body text, and a small quiet line for hints, counts and dates. context.Heading("North Point") context.Label("A white light every five seconds, seen from 18 nautical miles.") context.Caption("Last inspected in spring") A heading, a line of body text and a caption One line each: text does not wrap. A line too long for a box that clips ( Look{Clip: true} , a table cell) ends in "…". Sizes come from the theme: HeadingSize , TextSize , SmallTextSize . A screen reader reads texts beside each other in one box together, as one sentence. Text Any size, weight and colour, for the cases the three levels do not cover: a big figure with its unit, a code in a monospaced face, a state in its colour. theme := context.Theme context.Row(func() { context.Text("18", ui.TextStyle{Size: 32, Weight: draw2d.Bold}) context.Text("nm", ui.TextStyle{Size: 16, Color: theme.InkSoft}) }) context.Text("NP-0042", ui.TextStyle{Weight: draw2d.Mono}) // a code context.Text("Lamp failure", ui.TextStyle{Weight: draw2d.Medium, Color: theme.Danger}) // a state A large 18 with nm beside it, a code in monospace and a red state ui.TextStyle field Means Size Pixels; 0 = the theme's text size Weight draw2d.Regular , Medium , Bold , or Mono for codes and keys Color Zero = the theme's ink. Use the theme's tokens ( Danger , Warning , InkSoft ) so the dark theme follows Icon, IconSized A Lucide icon by name. Icon draws it at the theme's icon size in the soft ink; IconSized(name, size, colour) chooses both. theme := context.Theme context.Row(func() { context.Icon("lightbulb") context.Label("Lit") context.Spacer() context.IconSized("triangle-alert", 20, theme.Warning) context.Label("Foghorn silent") }) A bulb and Lit on the left, a warning triangle and Foghorn silent on the right An icon alone says nothing to a screen reader but its name ("triangle alert"): put words beside it, or describe the control it belongs to ( Describe ). Image A photo or any picture ( draw2d.Image ) filling a box, cropped evenly where their shapes differ, with rounded corners. Decode it once and keep it: the picture is uploaded once. //go:embed north-point.jpg var northPointFile []byte photo, err := draw2d.DecodeImage(bytes.NewReader(northPointFile)) // once, at the start … context.Image(photo, ui.Layout{Width: ui.Fixed(160), Height: ui.Fixed(100)}, 8) To show other pixels in it (a video's next frame), write them into photo.Pixels and call photo.Changed() . Tooltip Explains the control added just before it, in a small dark note, once the pointer rests on it for half a second (the theme's TooltipDelay ). For an icon button, it is the button's words. context.Row(func() { context.IconButton("rotate-ccw", "") context.Tooltip("Back to 18 nm and 5 s") }) A finger has no hover: on a phone, tooltips never show, so nothing important should be only in one. ← Components · Buttons →

components/text-fields.title: Text fields
components/text-fields.text: Text fields TextField(name, &text) and TextFieldWith(name, &text, options) edit your string in place, and return true on the frames it changes. The name is the field's id, not shown. A form A label column of its own width, then the fields. MaxLength caps what is typed, Weight: draw2d.Mono writes codes in a monospaced face, Width fixes a short field, Secret hides a password (a dot per character, nothing can be copied or cut). row := func(label string, field func()) { context.Row(func() { context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Fixed(90)}, func() { context.Label(label) }) field() }) } row("Name", func() { context.TextFieldWith("name", &name, ui.TextFieldOptions{MaxLength: 40}) }) row("Code", func() { context.TextFieldWith("code", &code, ui.TextFieldOptions{Weight: draw2d.Mono, Width: ui.Fixed(120)}) }) row("Password", func() { context.TextFieldWith("password", &password, ui.TextFieldOptions{Secret: true}) }) Name, Code in monospace and a hidden Password A search Nothing needs to "listen" to the field: the list below reads search in the same frame. context.TextFieldWith("search", &search, ui.TextFieldOptions{Placeholder: "Search lighthouses"}) found := 0 for _, name := range names { if strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(name), strings.ToLower(search)) { context.Label(name) found++ } } context.Caption(fmt.Sprintf("%d of %d", found, len(names))) A search box with cape, two results and 2 of 4 Placeholder shows, quiet, while the field is empty. To open a search ready to type in (a shortcut, a screen just shown), call context.FocusField("search") . Checking what was typed Say what is wrong right under the field, in the theme's danger colour, while it is wrong. context.TextFieldWith("name", &name, ui.TextFieldOptions{Placeholder: "Name", MaxLength: 40}) if strings.TrimSpace(name) == "" { context.Text("A lighthouse needs a name", ui.TextStyle{Size: context.Theme.SmallTextSize, Color: context.Theme.Danger}) } An empty Name field and A lighthouse needs a name in red Typing, everywhere To Do Place the caret, select Click; Shift-click; drag; double-click a word, triple-click all Move by words, to the ends Alt (Mac) or Ctrl with the arrows; Home, End Copy, cut, paste, select all Cmd or Ctrl with C, X, V, A Undo, redo Cmd/Ctrl+Z, Shift+Cmd/Ctrl+Z or Cmd/Ctrl+Y Finish Enter or a click elsewhere; Escape puts back the text it had when it took the keyboard Next field Tab, Shift+Tab: round the fields of the panel or sheet Accents and «ñ» type as anywhere (characters come after the keyboard layout). Pasted line breaks become spaces. On a phone the on-screen keyboard comes up, suggests words and underlines the one it composes; a finger held on a word selects it, with handles and a bar to cut, copy and paste. While a field has the keyboard, Go UI claims it, so a 3D view's shortcuts do not take the letters. FieldFocused(name) tells whether a field has it; Focus(path...) gives it to a field found by its scopes, with its text selected. ← Choices · Containers →

components/the-keyboard.title: Who has the keyboard

sections.text: An application that is only an interface

components/the-keyboard.text: Who has the keyboard This page is for whoever builds a program with go-ui and wants the keyboard to work for both the interface and whatever is behind it. At the end you will know which of the two modes to choose, and what a click, Tab, Enter, Space and Escape do in each. The problem Tab, Enter, Space and the arrows mean two things at once: To an interface , they move between buttons and press them, so someone who can't use a mouse can still use every control. To a game or a 3D view , they are its own controls: Space jumps, the arrows turn the camera, Tab shows the scores. Both can't have them. If the interface always took Space, a game would stop jumping and press whichever button was last clicked. So go-ui asks the program one question, through context.KeyboardNavigation : is there anything else that wants these keys? The two modes ui.WhenGiven (the default) ui.Always For a game, a 3D viewer, an editor over a scene a program that is only an interface: a register, a settings app Tab, Shift+Tab move between controls only while the interface has the keyboard always move between controls Enter, Space press the control Tab reached, while the interface has the keyboard press the control Tab reached A click on a button presses it, and leaves the keyboard where it was ; no ring presses it; no ring; the next Tab goes on from it Escape gives the keyboard back to the program (an open menu or dialog closes first) closes an open menu or dialog, or takes the ring off What the program reads every key while the interface does not have the keyboard none: the interface claims the keyboard all the time The interface has the keyboard while: a text field is typed in, a dialog or a sheet is open, or a menu or a select is open, Tab moved the focus while it had the keyboard (from a field to a button, say): it keeps it until Escape or a click, or the program gave it with context.TakeKeyboard() . With Always , it has the keyboard all the time. WhenGiven is the default because forgetting to choose then costs little: Tab doesn't walk the buttons. The other way round, a game that forgot would stop answering its own keys. A game over a 3D view Leave the mode alone. The game keeps its keys, and its pause menu takes the keyboard while it is open: if !paused && state.Pressed(input.KeyP) { paused = true context.TakeKeyboard() // Tab, Enter and Space now move through the menu } context.Begin(state) if paused { context.Panel("Paused", func() { if context.PrimaryButton("Resume") { paused = false context.ReleaseKeyboard() // the keys go back to the game } context.Button("Settings") }) } context.End() if paused && !context.HasKeyboard() { paused = false // Escape gave the keys back: resume, as Resume does } if !context.HasKeyboard() && state.Pressed(input.KeySpace) { ship.Jump() // Space is the game's whenever the menu doesn't have it } Pressing Escape in the menu gives the keyboard back too, and the game resumes on the next frame. HasKeyboard() stays true until the end of any frame in which the interface used Enter, Space or Escape, so the Space that pressed Resume is not also a jump. A click on Resume with the mouse presses it but takes nothing, so the Space that follows is a jump again. While the interface has the keyboard, go-ui claims it in the input state, as a text field always has, so go-renderer's viewer leaves its camera keys alone. context.WantsKeyboard() tells your own code the same thing. An application that is only an interface Set the mode once, before the first frame: context.KeyboardNavigation = ui.Always Now Tab goes through every button, check box, toggle, tab, select, chip and field in the order they are drawn, and comes round at the end. Shift+Tab goes back. Enter or Space presses the control Tab reached: it clicks a button, ticks a check box, picks a tab, opens a select. When the control with the focus goes away (a row deleted), the next Tab goes on from where it stood. A field reached by Tab selects its text, ready to be typed over. What Tab reaches Reached: Button and its variants, Selectable , Clickable , Checkbox , Toggle , Tabs (each tab), Select , Chip , TextField , NumberField (its number; the − and + buttons are skipped, since the number can be typed). A panel's fold button , in its title bar, comes before the panel's content. Inside a dialog or a sheet: Tab goes round its own controls only. Inside menus and lists: the arrows move, not Tab; that is unchanged. How the focus looks The ring only shows when the focus came from the keyboard. A click never shows it. The ring lies on the control's edge, with no gap, in Theme.FocusRing , Theme.FocusWidth wide (3 pixels by default). On a primary button it is drawn inside , in Theme.OnPrimary : a ring in the primary colour around a button of that colour could not be seen. A theme can also ask a field to light its own edge instead of drawing a ring around it ( Theme.FieldFocusEdge ), and a held control to shrink a little ( Theme.PressScale , 0.97 in Bubble). If the person asked the system for less motion, set context.LessMotion and held controls keep their size. The tokens are in a design system's look . What it costs While the interface does not have the keyboard, no control joins the Tab order, and a frame of three hundred controls takes about 1 % longer than before, from one comparison per control. While it has the keyboard, it takes up to 2.5 % longer. Neither allocates anything more. Moving the focus asks for one frame, so the ring shows at once even in an application that only draws when something changes. The measurements are in the performance audit . ← Components

get-started.title: Get started
get-started.text: Get started This page takes you from nothing to a window with a button that works, in about fifteen minutes. You need to know a little Go; you need no experience with interfaces. What you will do Install Go and a C compiler, which the window needs. Get Go UI and Go Renderer, side by side, and run an example. Write your first interface. ⚠️ Go UI is an educational project and its API still changes. Pin the commits you build against. 1. Install the tools You need Why How Go 1.25 or later The language go.dev/dl , then go version A C compiler The desktop window is opened through cgo Linux: gcc ; macOS: xcode-select --install ; Windows: MinGW-w64 on the PATH OpenGL 4.1 headers (Linux) What draws on Linux and Windows; macOS draws through Metal Debian, Ubuntu: sudo apt install libgl1-mesa-dev xorg-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev The library itself is pure Go: only programs that open a window need cgo. Tests do not, so go test ./... runs anywhere. 2. Get the code Go UI draws through Go Renderer , which Go downloads like any other module, at the version go.mod names: git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-ui cd go-ui go run ./cmd/app A whole desktop application opens: a menu bar, a toolbar with a search box, a list, a table and an inspector. Try go run ./cmd/app -dark , and the other examples: Example Shows go run ./cmd/app A desktop application with no 3D at all go run ./cmd/example Panels over a 3D scene go run ./cmd/scene-app An application layout around a 3D view go run ./cmd/workbench A grouped table, chips, a menu, a sheet, drag and drop go run ./cmd/plan-editor Editing a 3D scene: placing huts on an island's map 💡 No display? Add -capture shot.png to draw one frame into a picture; on a server, run it under xvfb-run . 3. Your first interface Make a module of your own and ask for Go UI, which brings Go Renderer with it: mkdir lighthouse && cd lighthouse go mod init example.com/lighthouse go get github.com/akrck02/go-ui@latest 💡 Changing Go UI or Go Renderer at the same time? Clone them beside your module and join the three with a workspace ( go work init . ../go-ui ../go-renderer ): Go then builds against your copies instead of the versions. main.go : package main import ( "log" ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" "github.com/akrck02/go-ui/window" ) func main() { lit := false // your data lives in your variables err := window.Run(window.Options{Title: "Lighthouse"}, func(context *ui.Context) { context.Heading("North Point") if context.PrimaryButton("Switch") { // true on the frame it is clicked lit = !lit } if lit { context.Label("The lamp is lit.") } }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } go mod tidy go run . Click the button: the line appears and goes. That is the whole idea of Go UI, called immediate mode : The function you give window.Run describes the interface , and runs again whenever something happens: a click, a key, the window resized. A control is a function call. A button returns true on the frame it is clicked; there are no button objects to create, keep or wire with callbacks. Your variables are the truth. Showing something is an if , a list is a for , and the screen can never show a stale value. Between frames the window sleeps: an idle Go UI program uses no processor. Where next If you want to… Read Learn step by step, building a register of lighthouses The tutorial Understand frames, layout, controls and themes in depth The guide Look up a control or an option The reference Put the interface over a 3D scene Lesson 6 Run it in a browser or on a phone In a web browser , on Android , Go UI for Android ← Documentation · Tutorial →

guides/controls.title: 🎛️ Controls
guides/controls.text: 🎛️ Controls Every control is a function call that adds a box and, for those you can act on, tells you what happened in this frame. Controls added inside a panel go in it; added outside any panel, they go on the screen . Text and icons Control What it does Label(text) , Heading(text) , Caption(text) , Text(text, style) Lines of text: body, bold title, small hint, or any size, weight and colour Icon(name) , IconSized(name, size, colour) A Lucide icon Image(picture, layout, radius) A picture ( draw2d.Image ) filling a box of the size given, cropped evenly where their shapes differ, its corners rounded Buttons Control What it does Button(label) , PrimaryButton(label) , IconButton(icon, label) Return true on the step they are clicked; an icon button with an empty label is square FlatButton(label) , FlatIconButton(icon, label) Buttons with no fill or border until hovered: menu bars and toolbars Selectable(icon, label, selected) An item that shows whether it is selected and returns true when clicked: full width in a column (a side list), fitted in a row (a group of tools) Clickable(name, layout, Looks{…}, content) Any box that reacts to the mouse, with its own looks when left alone, hovered and pressed: the building block for controls of your own, like a table row MenuButton(icon, label, content) , MenuItem(icon, label, hint) A flat button that opens a menu under it; see menus Choices and values Control What it does Checkbox(label, &value) A box to tick, with its label; clicking either flips the value. Returns true when it changes Toggle(label, &value) A settings row: the label on the left, a switch on the right Slider(name, &value, minimum, maximum) , SliderStep(…, step) A track with a knob: click to jump, drag to slide, Shift to slide ten times slower; SliderStep keeps whole steps NumberField(name, &value, minimum, maximum, step, format) A number with − and + on its sides; drag the number sideways for a step every 4 px, or click it to type a value (a point or a comma for decimals; Enter keeps it, Escape does not). The buttons and the drag keep whole steps; a typed value is kept as typed, and the program's own value is left alone until someone changes it. Shown with a format such as "%.1f s" Tabs(name, &selected, labels…) A segmented row, the selected segment raised; the program shows what belongs to it with an if Select(name, &selected, options) A field showing the chosen option; clicking opens the list over everything. Click an option, or use the arrows and Enter; Escape or a click elsewhere closes it TextField(name, &text) , TextFieldWith(name, &text, TextFieldOptions{…}) A line of text to type in, with a Placeholder , a MaxLength or a Width , Secret for a password (a dot for each character, nothing copied). Returns true on the steps the text changes; see text fields FieldFocused(name) , FocusField(name) Whether the field of a name has the keyboard (for a box the program draws around it), and giving it the keyboard (a search that opens ready to type in) Lists and scrolling Control What it does ScrollArea(name, layout, content) Content that scrolls when taller than the box: wheel or trackpad over it, or drag the thin bar on its right List(name, layout, count, rowHeight, row) A scroll area of equal rows that builds only the rows in sight: ten thousand rows cost what twenty do ListBox(name, layout, items, &selected) A scrolling list of selectable items Table(name, layout, columns, rows) A header and rows that scroll, with group captions and a selected row; see tables Rows, columns and grids Control What it does Row(content) , Column(content) Shortcuts for full-width boxes with the theme's gap; a row centres its children vertically Spacer() Takes the free space of its row or column, pushing what follows to the end Separator() A thin line across its row or column Grid(columns, content) Rows of equal cells (or any box with Layout.Columns ) Box(layout, content) , Frame(layout, look, content) Any box, arranged or also painted; see layout Chips, notes and gestures Control What it does Chip(icon, label, ChipLook{Fill, Ink}) A small rounded label (a tag, a state) in colours of your choice (zero = the theme's quiet ones); returns true when clicked RemovableChip(icon, label, look) A chip with a small ×: returns clicked, removed apart Tooltip(text) Explains the control added just before it, in a small dark note, once the pointer rests on it for half a second LongPressed() Tells whether the control added just before it was long-pressed in this frame: a finger held still on it for half a second, or the right mouse button. A touch that became a long press is no click Popover(name, &open, look, content) A box of the program's own floating under the control added just before it (a dropdown's choices); a touch outside, Escape or the back closes it Panels, sheets, dragging and resizing These have pages of their own, panels and layers and tables, dragging and resizing : Control What it does Panel(title, content) , PanelWith(title, PanelOptions{…}, content) A floating card with a title bar, moved, folded, placed, sized, locked or docked; see panels Sheet(title, SheetOptions{Width}, content) A modal card in the middle of the window; returns true when the person asks to close it. See sheets FilePicker(FilePickerOptions{…}) A sheet to choose a file or a folder on the disk; returns its path and true once it closes. See choosing a file DragSource(name, payload, layout, content) , DropTarget(name, layout, accepts, content) Drag a value of yours from one box to another, or onto the scene; see drag and drop Resizable(name, side, &size, minimum, maximum, layout, content) A box whose edge can be dragged to change its width or height; see resizable boxes Painting and motion Call What it does Context.Paint Adds a box the program paints itself once laid out, for shapes Go UI has no control for Context.Animate Eases a value to its target, asking for frames only while it moves Context.Appear Eases something in as it is shown Context.Fold Opens a box to its content's height and closes it to nothing, with motion (more under a list row)

guides/desktop.title: 🖥️ A window of its own
guides/desktop.text: 🖥️ A window of its own Package window opens a plain window with no 3D at all and runs the interface in it, painted on the theme's Background . The same program also runs in a web page and on Android . options := window.Options{Title: "Lighthouse register"} options.MinWidth, options.MinHeight = 960, 560 // the smallest the layout still works at options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) // -width, -height, -capture, -no-vsync, -dark, -continuous, -backend flag.Parse() window.Run(options, func(context *ui.Context) { context.Label("Hello") }) cmd/app is a complete example: a menu bar, a toolbar with filters and a search box, a navigation list, summary cards, a table whose rows are Clickable boxes with Share columns, an inspector with fields to rename a lighthouse and a status bar. Built for WebAssembly ( GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm ), the same program runs in a web page: the window is the page's canvas, drawn through WebGL2 ( in a web browser ); built for Android, it is the application's activity ( on Android ). The window's options Option Flag What it does Title The window's title (a page's title in a browser) Width , Height , MinWidth , MinHeight -width , -height The window's size (1280 × 800 when 0), and the smallest the layout still works at Continuous -continuous Draws every frame, for an interface that animates all the time Backend -backend automatic\|metal\|opengl What draws the window (below) CapturePath -capture file.png Draws one frame to a picture, in a hidden window, and returns NoVsync -no-vsync Draws as fast as possible instead of waiting for the display Dark -dark Starts in the dark theme Scene A 3D scene behind the interface (below) Canvas In a browser, the page's canvas to draw in ( web ) MaxFramesPerSecond , Hidden A cap on frames, and a function called when the program leaves the screen ( Android ) Drawing only when something happens The window draws only when something happens : input, a resize, a frame a control asks for (the caret's next blink, a tooltip coming due, through input.State.RequestFrame ), or window.Wake() , which a program calls from another goroutine when its data changes there. A frame that would look exactly like the one shown (the pointer moving over still parts, say) is not drawn either: the window compares the draw list's fingerprint with the last one. In between it sleeps: the register uses no processor while idle, against about 14% of a core drawing every frame. Options.Continuous ( -continuous ) draws every frame, for an interface that animates all the time. Over a 3D view ( viewer.Run ) the scene keeps drawing every frame. Measured in detail in performance and battery . A scene behind the interface Options.Scene puts a 3D scene behind the interface: a function called at every step, with the input the interface did not claim, that returns a scene and a camera (or nil for none). A drag on an empty part of the screen turns the camera while a drag on a slider moves the slider. Screens of every size On a phone, Context.Insets() says how much of each edge the system's bars cover, and Context.Size() gives the window's size, so a layout can paint under the bars and choose itself by the screen. The Android page has the rest of what a phone adds: the keyboard, notifications, the clipboard, preferences, films and the wallpaper's colours. Metal or OpenGL On macOS the window draws through Metal ; elsewhere through OpenGL 4.1. Options.Backend ( -backend automatic|metal|opengl ) chooses; if Metal cannot start, the window says so once and uses OpenGL. Both paint the same quads from the same atlas, and their captures match within 1/255 per channel. Metal needs less: with the register idle, its memory is 66–70 MB against 93–102 MB through OpenGL, and with a window that changes every frame it used about a third less processor, GPU and memory ( measurements ). The window has no depth or stencil buffer, which flat drawing never uses. Most of what the system then counts for the program is the window's own buffers, which grow with its size; the program itself (fonts, the atlas, its data) is about 25 MB.

guides/driving-a-window.title: 🎬 Driving a window
guides/driving-a-window.text: 🎬 Driving a window This page is for someone whose program should sometimes use itself: play a demo when nobody touches it, show a newcomer press here on the real button, replay what a person did to see the bug they reported, or check on a phone or a console what only the device does. At the end you will know how to write a script, give it to a window, record one, and read its report. The idea uitest already drives an interface with no display: it finds what was drawn by the name people see ("Light the lamp") and gives it input, frame by frame. Package uidrive is that same idea for a real window. A driver sits in the window loop: at each frame, after the window has gathered the real input and before your interface runs, it adds its own (a pointer, a finger, a key, typed text), and after your interface has drawn it may draw over it. Because both use the same code, a script that passes in go test does the same steps on a device. A script A script is plain text, one step a line. A person can read it, write it and change it in a pull request: # the lighthouse keeper's evening click "Add an entry" type "Fog at dawn" press Enter until "Saved" # waits for it to show, five seconds at most wait 0.5s tap "Light the lamp" hold "Lens" 1s # a long press drag "Boat" 120 0 # by a distance, in layout pixels drag "Boat" to "Harbour" # or onto another element scroll "Log" -3 # a negative amount goes down the page double-click "Entry" move-to "Help" # the pointer goes over it: a tooltip shows click-at 40 300 # a place, for what has no name press Shift+Tab Each step finds its element in what the last frame showed, as a screen reader would read it: a button by its text, a field by its placeholder, a line of text by what it says. A step that cannot find it ends the script with the same error codes uitest uses ( uitest.element-not-found , uitest.element-not-visible …). A script has no branches or loops on purpose: a program that needs logic writes Go. uidrive.Parse reads a script; a line it does not understand is an error with the code uidrive.script-not-read and its line number. Script.String writes one back. Giving it to a window script, err := uidrive.Parse(text) if err != nil { return err } player := uidrive.Play(script, uidrive.PlayOptions{Report: os.Stdout, Show: true}) return window.Run(window.Options{Title: "Lighthouse", Driver: player}, build) With Show: true the player draws what it does over the interface: an outline around the element its step found, the pointer as an orange ring (filled while pressed) and each finger as a dot, so a demo or a tutorial is seen, not only run. Here the register example ( go run ./cmd/app -script tour.txt ) has typed "Rock" in its search box and points at New lighthouse : The register driven by a script: the search box says Rock, and an orange outline and ring point at New lighthouse go run ./cmd/app -record session.txt writes down what you do instead (see below). window.Options.Driver works on every target: the desktop, a web page, Android and the 3DS. The window keeps drawing while the script plays, even one that draws only on demand, and goes back to sleeping when it ends. player.Done() and player.Err() tell how it went. A window with no driver pays nothing for it: no allocation and no work in its frames ( BenchmarkAWindowStepWithoutADriver in window ). The person wins Any input that comes from a person while a script plays (a key, a click, the pointer moving, a touch) stops it at once: the player lets go of whatever it held, so no button stays pressed, and ends with uidrive.script-stopped . An attract mode stops the moment someone picks the device up. Automatic modes A demo (attract mode): a script that shows the program's best parts, with Show: true . Start it after a while without input; a touch gives the program back. A replay : record what a person did (below), and play it back to see what they saw. A tutorial : the same, a step at a time. A program can play a script of one move-to to point at the control to press, and let the person press it. A test on the device : play a script with a Report , and read the report from the device's log (below). Recording a session uidrive.Recorder is a driver that adds nothing: it watches what a person does and writes it down as steps, by the names of what they pressed. Give it to the window, and save recorder.Script() when the window closes ( Options.Hidden ): recorder := uidrive.Record() options := window.Options{Driver: recorder, Hidden: func() { _ = os.WriteFile("session.txt", []byte(recorder.Script().String()), 0o644) // a lost recording is not worth stopping for }} Played back, the script does the same. Because it names elements rather than places, it still works when the layout moves. A press on something with no name is written as a click-at its place; a drag that starts on something with no name is left out, since a script could not find where to start it again. The report With PlayOptions.Report set, the player writes a line for each step and one at the end, each starting with uidrive: so a test runner finds them among the device's other logs: uidrive: step 1 ok: click "Add an entry" uidrive: step 2 failed uitest.element-not-found: click "Remove": no element "Remove" in the last frame; it showed […] uidrive: script failed at step 2: uitest.element-not-found Give it standard output on a computer, the console on a 3DS, and a writer to Android's log on a phone. A script that passes ends with uidrive: script passed: 5 steps .

guides/getting-started.title: 🚀 Getting started
guides/getting-started.text: 🚀 Getting started Go UI draws interfaces over a Go Renderer view. This page explains how a frame works, shows the examples that come with it, and how what you describe ends up on the screen. A frame In immediate mode there are no button objects to create, keep and update. Each update step, the program calls the controls again, with its own variables: interfaceContext.Begin(state) // the step's mouse and keyboard interfaceContext.Panel("Lighthouse", func() { interfaceContext.Heading(light.Name) if interfaceContext.PrimaryButton("Switch on") { // true on the step it is clicked light.On = true } }) interfaceContext.End() // lay out, paint, claim the mouse Showing or hiding something is an if ; a list is a for . The interface holds none of your data, so it can never show a stale value. What it does remember between frames is small and keyed by each control's id : which control is being pressed, where a panel was dragged, whether it is folded. Call Begin and End in every update step (the function given to viewer.Run ), and set world.Overlay.Drawing = interfaceContext.Drawing() once, so Go Renderer paints the result. Ids and scopes An id is a hash of the control's label and of the scopes around it. Panels open a scope with their title, so two "Apply" buttons in different panels do not mix. Inside a loop, open a scope per item with Push(name) and Pop() . Anything after ## in a label is part of the id but not shown: "Switch off##switch" and "Switch on##switch" are the same button with different words. Call What it does Push(name) , Pop() Open and close a scope, so controls with the same label in a loop stay apart "Label##id" Words after ## are part of the id but not shown Area(path…) Where a control was drawn in the last frame, by its scopes and label ( Area("Properties", "Apply") ): to place something next to it, or to click it in a test The examples Every example accepts the window's flags: -width , -height , -dark for the dark theme, and -capture file.png to draw one frame to a picture and exit ( go run ./cmd/<name> -h lists the rest). go run ./cmd/app # the application above (-dark for the dark theme) go run ./cmd/scene-app # the same kind of layout around a 3D view go run ./cmd/plan-editor # place huts on an island's map go run ./cmd/workbench # a grouped table, chips, a menu, a sheet, drag and drop go run ./cmd/example # a panel over a scene go run ./cmd/example -capture shot.png go run ./cmd/mobile -width 400 -height 860 cmd/web is the scene example put together for a browser ( web ); cmd/mobile builds into an Android app ( Android ). The library itself needs no cgo; the examples do, as they open a Go Renderer window. The tests need no display: they measure text with a fake measurer. go vet ./... go test ./... go test -run xxx -bench . # a frame of three hundred controls How it is drawn At End the laid-out boxes become commands of a draw2d.List (rounded rectangles, shadows, lines of text, icons), each panel on its own layer and its content clipped to it. Go Renderer paints that list after the scene, in the same pass and atlas as its labels, so the whole interface is one draw call. Text is measured with Go Renderer's own fonts ( overlay.NewMeasurer ) at the screen's density, so what is laid out is exactly what is painted. A program with fonts of its own (a brand's) sets window.Options.Fonts : the window measures and paints in them (and a program that makes its interface itself uses ui.NewInFonts with the same fonts). A frame of three panels with three hundred controls builds, lays out and paints in about 0.1 ms ( go test -bench . ). More in performance and battery . Next: layout , then the controls .

guides/input.title: 🖱️ Mouse, keyboard and touch
guides/input.text: 🖱️ Mouse, keyboard and touch Go UI shares the mouse and the keyboard with what is behind it: a 3D view's camera, the viewer's shortcuts. This page says who gets them, and how fingers are followed on a touch screen. Who gets the mouse Controls react to the mouse using where they were laid out in the previous frame (sizes are only known at End ). The pointer is a frame behind what is drawn, which nobody notices at sixty frames a second. Hover : the front-most panel under the pointer is the only one whose controls can be hovered. Within it, the first control to find the pointer over it takes it; containers that react to the mouse (a title bar) look after their content, so the buttons inside them win. Press and click : a pressed control keeps the mouse until the button is let go, even if the pointer strays. A click is a press and a release over the same control. The scene keeps its drags : a press on empty screen belongs to the camera until it is let go; panels it passes over do not take it. Claims : at End , when the pointer is over a panel or a control is pressed, the interface calls state.ClaimMouse() . Go Renderer's viewer then gives its cameras and shortcuts the input without the mouse, so dragging inside a panel does not turn the view. A text field with the focus claims the keyboard the same way. WantsMouse() and WantsKeyboard() tell your own code. Pointer shape : a hand over buttons, four arrows over a title bar that can be dragged and while dragging a payload, an I-beam over a text field, a two-headed arrow over a resize handle. Modal and dragging : while a sheet is open or a payload is dragged, the interface claims the mouse and the keyboard wherever the pointer is. Which layer is in front, and so gets the mouse first, is drawn in panels and layers . Fingers On a touch screen, one finger is followed from where it comes down: the way it goes first decides who takes it, the innermost scroll area for up and down, a SwipeBox for sideways (pages, cards in a row, a row swiped away), and the control it came down on is then not touched. A finger that stays still on a control for half a second long-presses it ( LongPressed ). Call What it does SwipeBox(name, layout, axis, content) Takes sideways swipes: pages, cards in a row, a row swiped away LongPressed() Whether the control just added was long-pressed: a finger held still for half a second, or the right mouse button ScrollPull(name) Measures a pull past a list's top, for a list that refreshes ScrollOffset(name) How far an area is scrolled, for a bar that shrinks over it Context.Touches() The fingers on a touch screen, for a control of a program's own that follows them (an on-screen stick); the first finger is also the pointer that clicks Context.Back Answers a phone's back gesture; modals and sheets answer it first Scroll areas glide on when let go. How touches reach Go UI on a phone is in Android .

guides/layout.title: 📐 Layout
guides/layout.text: 📐 Layout Every control is a box , and boxes nest. Layout happens in End , once the whole tree is known, so a box can grow into space that depends on boxes declared after it. Asking for a layout A box's Layout says: Field Meaning Direction Horizontal (children left to right, the default) or Vertical (top to bottom) Width , Height Fit() (as big as the content, the default), Grow() / GrowBy(weight) (the content plus a share of the free space), Share(weight) (a share of the free space, starting from nothing: equal shares come out equal, so table columns line up), Fixed(pixels) , Percent(share) ; .Between(min, max) bounds any of them Padding Space inside the edges: Pad(all) , PadXY(horizontal, vertical) or each side Gap Space between children AlignX , AlignY Start , Center or End : where children sit when there is room to spare Columns Above 0, a grid: children fill rows of this many equal cells, with Gap both ways Wrap On a horizontal box, children that would pass the right edge go on to a new line, like words (a row of tags); give the box a width that does not follow its content ( Grow in a column, Fixed ) interfaceContext.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Gap: 8}, func() { … }) interfaceContext.Frame(layout, ui.Look{Fill: theme.Surface, Border: theme.Line, BorderWidth: 1, Radius: 6}, func() { … }) Box only arranges; Frame also paints a fill, a border, rounded corners, a shadow or a clip ( Look ). Because layouts and looks are plain structs, they can come from a file one day, like a theme. When a fill and a border are not enough, Look.Backdrop draws the rest of a box's background itself: anything with a Paint(area, drawing) method, called under the box's children. A pixel-art window (an outline, a frame of two colours, corners cut a pixel at a time) or a patterned panel is a backdrop. Keep one value of it and point every look at it, so a frame allocates nothing. Text can carry a hard shadow the same way pixel-art games draw it: TextStyle{Shadow: colour} draws it a pixel right and down, under the text. How sizes are worked out The work is done one axis at a time: Fit , from the leaves up: a text is as wide as it measures, an icon as its size; a box adds up its children along its direction (plus gaps) or takes the biggest across it, plus padding. Grow , from the root down: percentages take their share of the parent; along the direction, growing children split the space left in proportion to their weights; across it, they take the parent's size. When the content does not fit (a narrow window), the growing children shrink instead, each giving up part of what it has above its minimum, so fixed and fitted boxes around them (a side column, an inspector, a button) keep their size. Place , from the root down, with padding, gaps and alignment. Text does not wrap yet, so heights never depend on widths, except in a box with Wrap : its height is worked out once the widths are known, which the axis-by-axis order allows. Content that still does not fit overflows at the end and is cut by the panel. A line of text in a box whose look clips ( Look{Clip: true} , like a table cell) ends in "…" where it would pass the box's edge. A whole application The same boxes lay out a whole window. Here the register ( cmd/app ) is a column of a menu bar, a toolbar and a row; the row holds a fixed navigation list, a growing middle (cards in Share columns over a table) and a fixed inspector. Narrow the window and only the middle shrinks. Shortcuts for the common cases ( Row , Column , Spacer , Separator , Grid ) are in the controls .

guides/panels-and-layers.title: 🗂️ Panels and layers
guides/panels-and-layers.text: 🗂️ Panels and layers An interface is made of layers, drawn one over another. What is in front is drawn last and gets the mouse first. Panels Control What it does Panel(title, content) A floating card with a title bar: drag the bar to move it, the chevron folds it. Pressing a panel brings it to the front. PanelWith(title, PanelOptions{…}, content) The same, placed ( X , Y ), sized ( Width , Height ), Locked , or docked to an edge ( DockLeft , DockRight , DockTop , DockBottom ) Panels open a scope with their title, so controls with the same label in two panels stay apart ( ids and scopes ). The screen Controls added outside any panel go on the screen , a box the size of the window behind every panel: a status bar is a Spacer() followed by a full-width Frame . The screen can hold a whole application layout: boxes painted with a fill there (bars, side columns) take the mouse like panels do, and a growing box left transparent lets a 3D view show through, with the camera working inside it ( cmd/scene-app ). Editing the scene it shows A program that edits the scene it shows runs through Go Renderer's viewer.Edit : the interface is built in its function, and viewer.View turns the pointer into a point on the ground. cmd/plan-editor places huts on an island by clicking on the map (a drag still moves the map), and a panel lists them to select, rename and remove; at rest it uses no processor or GPU. Popups The list of a select, a menu and a tooltip are popups : boxes that float over everything, next to the control that opened them, under it or above it when there is no room below. Popups are drawn above every panel and get the mouse before them. An open select also takes the keyboard (for its arrows) until it closes. Popover makes a popup of the program's own ( controls ). Menus context.MenuButton("plus", "Add", func() { if context.MenuItem("box", "Hut", "") { addHut() } context.Separator() if context.MenuItem("copy", "Copy", "Ctrl+D") { copySelected() } }) The menu is a popup, like a select's list: it opens under its button, or above it when there is no room. Items are chosen with a click, or with the arrows and Enter; choosing closes it, and so do Escape and a click anywhere else. While it is open it holds the keyboard. The hint is drawn quietly on the right: the text of a shortcut, which the program handles itself. Sheets if confirming && context.Sheet("Remove part", ui.SheetOptions{}, func() { context.Label("Remove the lens from the list?") if context.PrimaryButton("Remove") { removeLens(); confirming = false } }) { confirming = false // Escape, the × or a click on the dimmed backdrop } A sheet is shown with an if , as long as the program wants. It dims everything behind it and takes the mouse and the keyboard: nothing behind reacts, a field behind loses the focus when the sheet opens, Tab goes round the sheet's own fields, and End claims both, so cameras and shortcuts keep still. It returns true on the step the person asks to close it: Escape (unless a field, a select or a menu inside it takes Escape first), the × in its title or a click on the backdrop. SheetOptions.Width sizes the card (420 px by default). Popups (a select inside the sheet) open over it. The dimming colour is the theme's Scrim . Choosing a file A file picker is a sheet made for one question: which file, or which folder? Its left column has places to start from (the home folder, the disk's root, and the folders the program offers), the right one what the folder open holds, folders first, and the row above the folder's path, to go up or type a path straight in. if picking { path, closed := context.FilePicker(ui.FilePickerOptions{ Title: "Choose a model", Start: modelPath, // opens beside the file chosen before Suffixes: []string{".glb"}, // the folders always show, to go through them Places: []string{"/opt"}, }) if closed { picking = false if path != "" { modelPath = path } } } A click on a folder goes into it. A click on a file chooses it, and a second click, or Choose , ends the picker with it; Cancel , Escape or the backdrop end it with nothing. With Folder: true it chooses a folder instead: Choose takes the one open, and files are not shown. Hidden files (a dot first) show only when asked. It is drawn like every other control, so it looks the same on every system and asks nothing of the system's own dialogs. ReadFolder lets a test give it a folder of its own. Modals and overlays Context.Modal and Context.Overlay put a program's own content over everything, dimming what is behind (a dialog) or not (a note at the bottom). A modal covers the overlays, as a dialog or a drawer covers a phone's floating buttons: they are not touched nor read while it is open. With LayerOptions.Leave they leave with motion once the program stops showing them, fading and moving away (a picture of their last frame, which cannot be touched). Context.Back answers a phone's back gesture; modals and sheets answer it first.

guides/screen-readers.title: 🗣️ Screen readers

sections.text: Describing a control of your own

guides/screen-readers.text: 🗣️ Screen readers A screen reader speaks what is on the screen for a person who cannot see it, and lets them act on it: on a phone, TalkBack reads what a finger moves over, and a double tap presses it. It needs the screen as things with names , not pixels. While one is on ( SetScreenReader(true) , which the window does on Android), every frame also makes a list of what can be read, worked out from the boxes themselves, at no cost while none is on. How the boxes are read A control is a node , read by the texts inside it: a button reads "Light the lamp, button". A control inside another (a switch in a row) is a node of its own, inside the row. Texts beside each other in one box are read together : a row's title and the line under it are one node, and a paragraph is one, not a node per word. A scroll area holds its rows , and only those that show are read; the screen reader can scroll it on ( ReaderForward ) or back. What is behind a modal or a sheet is left out , as it cannot be touched. The node the screen reader is on is ringed ( SetScreenReaderFocus ), dark outside and light inside, over everything, as a phone rings what TalkBack reads. Describing a control of your own The controls say what they are and their state: a checkbox ticked, a toggle on (a switch), the tab shown, a slider's range, a field's text (not a secret one's). Describe says it for a control of your own, after it, in every frame: if interfaceContext.Clickable("beacon", layout, looks, drawSwitch) { beacon = !beacon } interfaceContext.Describe(ui.Description{Role: ui.SwitchRole, Label: "Beacon", Checked: beacon}) What Describe leaves empty stays as the boxes tell it. Hidden leaves out a decoration, or a label read already with the field it names. A control with an icon alone and no label is read by the Tooltip that follows it ("Go back"), as the pointer's note already says what it does. With no tooltip it is read by the icon's name ("arrow left") for want of a better one: describe it with what it does. After a menu button or a select, Describe describes the button, even while its list is open over it. What the screen reader asks Call What it does SetScreenReader(on) Makes the list of nodes every frame while a screen reader is on SetScreenReaderFocus(id) Rings the node the screen reader is on ScreenReaderAct(id, action) Done in the next frame: a press clicks the control as a tap would (a field takes the keyboard), a long press is read by LongPressed , forward and backward scroll an area or move a slider a step ScreenReaderSetText(id, text) Text the screen reader types, pastes or dictates into a field: the field takes it whole, as typing (one line, cut at its MaxLength ), and the keyboard stays down Nodes keep their ids from frame to frame, so the screen reader stays on what it was reading. On Android, the window hands the list to Go Renderer, which gives it to TalkBack ( Android ).

guides/tables-and-dragging.title: 📋 Tables, dragging and resizing
guides/tables-and-dragging.text: 📋 Tables, dragging and resizing cmd/workbench puts the pieces of an editor together around a 3D view: a list of a lighthouse's parts on the left, an inspector with tags on the right, a menu to add a part, and a sheet that asks before removing one.
