Both columns can be resized by their inner edge. go run ./cmd/workbench # -demo menu, -demo sheet or -demo drag open them for a capture Tables columns := []ui.Column{ {Title: "Part", Width: ui.Share(1)}, {Title: "Code", Width: ui.Fixed(64)}, {Title: "Count", Width: ui.Fixed(56), Align: ui.End}, // numbers on the right } context.Table("parts", ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, columns, func(table *ui.Table) { for index, part := range parts { if index == 0 || part.group != parts[index-1].group { table.Group(part.group) // a caption in small capitals, across the columns } if table.Row(part.key, index == selected, part.name, part.code, strconv.Itoa(part.count)) { selected = index } } }) The header stays while the rows scroll. A selected row is tinted, with a strip of the primary colour on its left; Row returns true when clicked. Fixed and Share widths make the header and every row line up; text that does not fit its cell ends in "…". Rows and captions have fixed heights, so the table counts the ones out of sight without building them: the loop still runs over every row each step (a function call each, and the cells' strings are the program's), but only the dozen or so in sight become boxes. A few thousand rows are fine. Give the table a height that does not follow its content, or every row is built. Cells are text; Go Renderer has one typeface, so there is no monospaced column yet. Drag and drop context.DragSource("Painted", tagPainted, ui.Layout{}, func() { context.Chip("tag", "Painted", look) }) isTag := func(payload any) bool { _, ok := payload.(tagName); return ok } if payload, dropped := context.DropTarget("part tags", layout, isTag, showTags); dropped { addTag(payload.(tagName)) } context.End() // the scene's side, after End if drag, dragging := context.Dragging(); dragging && drag.OverScreen { previewAt(groundAt(drag.X, drag.Y)) // where it would land, with viewer.View.PointOnGround } if drop, dropped := context.DroppedOnScreen(); dropped { placeAt(groundAt(drop.X, drop.Y), drop.Payload) } Call What it does DragSource(name, payload, layout, content) A box that can be dragged, carrying a value of yours; returns true when clicked instead DropTarget(name, layout, accepts, content) A box that takes the payloads accepts says (nil takes any); returns the payload on the step it is let go there Dragging() The payload, the pointer and whether it is over the open screen, during a drag DroppedOnScreen() A payload let go over the open screen, with the pointer's place Any box can be a drag source carrying a value of yours ( any ). A press on it that moves four pixels or more becomes a drag; less is a click, which DragSource returns, so a chip inside can still be clicked. Buttons inside keep their clicks too, but a drag that starts on them takes the mouse from them. While dragging, the source's name follows the pointer in a small label, the pointer shows four arrows (Go Renderer has no closed-hand shape), and the interface holds the mouse and the keyboard, so cameras stay still and Escape cancels the drag. A drop target is a box that takes payloads: accepts says which (nil takes any). While one it takes is over it, it is highlighted; on the step it is let go there, DropTarget returns it. With targets inside targets, the innermost under the pointer takes the drop. Let go over the open screen (no panel, no painted box, no target) and the payload is the program's: DroppedOnScreen reports it with the pointer's place on the step of the release, from Begin to the next Begin , so it can be asked after End , next to the scene's code. During the drag, Dragging tells the payload, the pointer and whether it is over the open screen, to preview the drop on the scene. Resizable boxes context.Resizable("parts", ui.RightSide, &sideWidth, 240, 520, ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { … }) A resizable box has a handle on one side ( RightSide for a column on the left of the window, LeftSide for one on the right, BottomSide and TopSide for strips): a thin line, drawn like a separator, that turns the primary colour and shows the resize pointer under the mouse. Dragging it writes the new width or height into your variable, kept between the minimum and the maximum (0 = no maximum); the program keeps the variable and can save it. The layout's size along the handle comes from the variable; the rest of the layout applies to the content.

guides/testing-an-interface.title: 🧪 Testing an interface

sections.text: Seeing the results in a window

guides/testing-an-interface.text: 🧪 Testing an interface This page is for someone building a program on Go UI who wants go test to check its interface: press its buttons, type in its fields and see what it shows, with no display. At the end you will know how to open a test window, act in it, find what it drew and read its errors. The shortest test Package uitest opens a pretend window. It runs your interface function frame by frame, exactly as a real window does, but nothing is painted and no screen is needed. It works in CI too. package log_test import ( "testing" ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" "github.com/akrck02/go-ui/uitest" ) func TestAddingANoteShowsItInTheLog(t *testing.T) { note, entries := "", []string{} window, err := uitest.New(func(context *ui.Context) { context.TextField("note", &note) if context.Button("Add") { entries = append(entries, note) note = "" } for _, entry := range entries { context.Label(entry) } }) if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } window.Frame() // the first frame gives every control its place window.Context().Focus("note") window.Type("Fog at dawn") if err := window.Click("Add"); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } if _, err := window.Element("Fog at dawn"); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } } The test passes: the note is in the log. The same code, with its output checked, is ExampleWindow in the package. Why run a frame first? Go UI is immediate-mode: a control learns where it is when the frame ends. Before the first frame nothing has a place, so nothing can be clicked. The window uitest.New(build, options...) takes your interface function and some options: Option Default What it changes Size(width, height) 800 × 600 The window, in layout pixels Scale(factor) 1 Framebuffer pixels per layout pixel (2 on most phones) Theme(theme) ui.LightTheme() The theme Measurer(measurer) FixedMeasurer How text is measured Test(t) none Names the window after its test, so the results viewer can show it (below) FixedMeasurer makes every character half the text size wide. Real fonts differ from machine to machine; fixed widths make a layout the same everywhere, so a test that passes on your laptop passes in CI. Frame() runs one frame, Frames(count) several. Resize changes the size between frames. Acting in it Every action runs whole frames, so the interface sees it as it would on a screen. What Methods The pointer MoveTo , MoveToElement , Press , Release , Click , ClickAt , DoubleClick , Drag , DragElement , Scroll The keyboard PressKey , HoldKey , ReleaseKey , Tab , ShiftTab , Type (all in one frame), TypeOneByOne Touch TouchDown , TouchMove , TouchUp , Tap , LongPress Time Wait(duration) A click is a move, a press and a release. Go UI answers a button when it is let go, as desktops do, so the release frame is the one where Button returns true. After each input the window runs one more frame, and any frame the interface asked for at once, as a real window does. So what a click changed is on screen when Click returns, even when it was drawn before the button: a tab bar at the bottom that changes the page above it. Time stands still The window has its own clock, and only Wait moves it. Frames(100) takes no time at all, so a long press never happens by accident. Wait(time.Second) runs a frame every sixtieth of a second until a second has passed, which is what long presses, double clicks and animations need. Every run gives the same result, however slow the machine. Finding what it drew Element(label) finds a control, a text or a scroll area in the last frame, by the name a screen reader would read: a button's text, a described label, a line of text. You get back: Field Rect Where it was laid out, in layout pixels Visible Some of it shows: not scrolled away, not behind a dialog Focused It has the focus ( ui.Context.FocusedID ) Pressable A click does something to it Two buttons called "Save" in different panels? ElementWithin("North", "Save") finds the one inside the panel whose title is "North": inside the smallest painted box (a panel, a card) that holds the outer element. ElementIn("north", "Save") does it by the scopes given to Push , outermost first, when you know them. A button with only an icon is found by the Tooltip that follows it: Click("Add a lighthouse") . Texts() lists every line drawn, in order, and DrawList() gives the whole draw list, for tests about colours and shapes. Playing a script A test can also play a script : the same few lines a real window plays for a demo or a tutorial (see Driving a window ). uidrive.Parse reads it and Play runs it, a sixtieth of a second a frame on the window's clock, and returns the error of the first step that failed: script, err := uidrive.Parse(` click "Note" # a field is found by its placeholder type "Fog at dawn" click "Add" until "Fog at dawn" 1s `) if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } if err := window.Play(script); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } Both use one piece of code to find elements and make input (package uidrive ), so a script that passes here does the same steps on a device. uitest.Driver gives the window any other driver, which it runs at every frame as a real window does. Errors Nothing in uitest panics or fails your test for you: methods return errors, and you decide. Every error has a code, which a program checks with errors.Is or uitest.CodeOf , never by its text: Code When uitest.element-not-found No element has that label; the message lists the labels on screen uitest.element-ambiguous Several have it: use ElementIn uitest.element-not-visible It is scrolled away or behind a dialog, so it cannot be clicked uitest.element-not-pressable It is only text: a click would do nothing uitest.invalid-size A window with no width or no height uitest.recording-not-saved , uitest.recording-not-read A recording for the viewer could not be written or read err := window.Click("Remove") if errors.Is(err, uitest.ErrorElementNotFound) { // the log has no Remove button yet } Seeing the results in a window When a test fails, it helps to see what its window showed. Make the window with Test(t) : window, err := uitest.New(build, uitest.Test(t)) Then run your tests through the viewer instead of go test : go run github.com/akrck02/go-ui/cmd/uitest ./... go run github.com/akrck02/go-ui/cmd/uitest -dark ./editor/... -run TestSaving It runs go test with the arguments you give, with recording on, and opens a Go UI window. Every test it ran is listed on the left by package, failed ones first; the chips above it ( All , Failed , With a window , each with how many) narrow the list. A test with no window shows what it wrote. A window test shows its error codes and messages, and a replay of its frames. Play shows them one after another, a tenth of a second each, and stops at the last; Pause holds the frame shown. Step through them with Previous frame , Next frame or the slider. The pointer is a ring, filled while pressed; fingers are orange dots; the element an action found has an outline in the theme's focus colour. Click an error's code to jump to the frame it came after. From another module, name the viewer's version: go run github.com/akrck02/go-ui/cmd/uitest@main ./... (add GOPROXY=direct when the module proxy has not seen the latest main yet). Recording costs nothing in a plain go test : a window only keeps its frames while the UITEST_RECORD variable names a folder, which the viewer sets for you. The replay shows the test's window at its own size (smaller only when it does not fit), on its theme's background. The test measured text with its own measurer and the viewer paints with real fonts, so each recording keeps how wide every line was measured, and the viewer shrinks a line that would come out wider: the frame looks as the test laid it out. The viewer needs a display. What it cannot do yet There is no picture of a frame without a display: Go Renderer cannot paint without one yet. Read DrawList() instead, or look at the frames in the viewer.

guides/text-fields.title: ⌨️ Text fields
guides/text-fields.text: ⌨️ Text fields A text field edits your string as it is typed: TextField("Name", &entry.name) changes entry.name on the step a key is pressed, and returns true then. go run ./cmd/app -demo-search north types in the search box on its second step, as above. Keys To Do Place the caret Click; Shift-click selects up to there Select Drag; double-click for a word, triple-click for the whole text Move Arrows; with Alt on a Mac or Ctrl elsewhere, a word at a time; Home and End (or Cmd+arrows on a Mac) to the ends. Shift selects as it moves Delete Backspace and Delete; a word with Alt (Mac) or Ctrl Copy, cut, paste, select all Cmd on a Mac or Ctrl elsewhere, with C, X, V, A Undo, redo Cmd/Ctrl+Z, and Shift+Cmd/Ctrl+Z or Cmd/Ctrl+Y. Typing a run of letters, or of Backspaces, is undone in one step; each field keeps its own history while it has the focus End the edit Enter, or a click anywhere else; Escape puts back the text the field had when it took the focus Go to the next field Tab, or Shift+Tab to go back; it goes round, includes number fields, and selects the text it lands on Characters come from the system after the keyboard layout and dead keys, so accents and «ñ» type as anywhere else. Line breaks and tabs pasted in become spaces: the field has one line. Text longer than the field slides sideways to keep the caret in sight. Focus Focus(path…) gives the keyboard to a field by its scopes and label, as Area finds it, with its text selected: the search box on a shortcut, or the first field of a form that just opened. While a field has the focus, End claims the keyboard, so the viewer's shortcuts and cameras do not take the letters. By the field's name instead, FieldFocused(name) tells whether it has the keyboard and FocusField(name) gives it the keyboard. On a phone A phone's on-screen keyboard edits the field's text rather than typing key by key: it suggests words, keeps the word it is still making underlined ( composing ) and deletes around the caret. TypedField() tells the window which field is typed in, with its text, selection and composing word, and EditTypedField(edit) puts the keyboard's edit in, in the next frame, as typing: one line, cut at MaxLength , its words undone as typed ones are. A key or a touch that changes the text ends the composing. The Android window does both ( Android ). On a touch screen, text is chosen as on a phone. A finger held on a word selects it: a drop-shaped handle hangs under each end of the selection, and a bar over it offers Cut , Copy , Paste and Select all ( SetEditingWords in the person's language, EditingWords to read them; a secret field cannot be cut or copied). A touch shows a handle under the caret. A finger drags a handle to move its end, or the caret; the handle hangs under the text, so the finger does not hide what it chooses, and the ends never cross. The handles and the bar are popups of the field's own: pressing them keeps the field typed in. Typing, on either keyboard, puts them away; a mouse has none.

guides/themes.title: 🎨 Themes
guides/themes.text: 🎨 Themes Every control reads its colours and sizes from interfaceContext.Theme : surfaces, inks, lines, the primary colour, the scrim behind sheets, text sizes, control height, gaps, padding, corner radii and the shadow. LightTheme() is the default; DarkTheme() has the same sizes with dark colours. Change a token and every control follows. Every example takes -dark to start in the dark theme. window.SystemPrefersDark() tells whether the phone or the browser is set to a dark theme, so a program can follow it (on the desktop it says no for now) ( Android ). On Android 12 and later, window.SystemPalettes() returns the five palettes the phone makes from the wallpaper, to build a theme from them ( Android ).

overview.title: Welcome to Go UI 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go UI 👋 Go UI makes the parts of a program you click and type in : buttons, panels, lists, forms, menus. Over a 3D scene, or as a whole application in a window, a web page or a phone. A program made with Go UI describes its whole screen again many times a second from its own data ( a title, then a button, then a list of these things ), and Go UI draws it and tells the program what was clicked. So the screen can never show something out of date. Is it for me? ✅ You write Go and want buttons and panels over a Go Renderer scene. ✅ You want a desktop application in Go, that also runs in a web page and on Android. ✅ You are learning how interfaces are made. ❌ You want a ready-made app without programming: Go UI is for building them. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time just want to see what it looks like Try it without writing code 2 min are new to it and want to install it Get started 15 min want to learn step by step 🏴‍☠️ The quest : a register of lighthouses, in 7 levels 2 h want to know how something works (layout, text fields, themes) The guides — want to use one control (a button, a table, a sheet) Components : each one with real examples — are looking up a method or an option The reference — Try it without writing code With Go installed and the projects copied (see Get started ), these open finished examples: go run ./cmd/app # a desktop application (add -dark for the dark theme) go run ./cmd/example # panels over a 3D island go run ./cmd/workbench # a table, chips, a menu, drag and drop All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page Get started : install, the examples, your first interface Learn The quest : seven levels that build a register of lighthouses Understand The guides, one subject each: Getting started : a frame, ids and scopes, how it is drawn Layout : boxes, Fit , Grow , Share , how sizes are worked out Controls : text, buttons, choices, lists, grids, chips, painting Panels and layers : panels, popups, menus, sheets, modals Tables, dragging and resizing Text fields : typing, selecting, focus, a phone's keyboard Mouse, keyboard and touch Themes : the tokens, light and dark Screen readers A window of its own : interfaces without a scene Testing an interface : go test presses, types and looks, with no display Driving a window : scripts that play a demo, a tutorial or a replay in a real window, and tests on the device Use Components : every control, with examples and pictures Reference The reference : the context's methods by purpose, every type Platforms In a web browser On Android On the Nintendo 3DS The project Performance and battery audit Words you will meet Word What it means Go A programming language. To try these projects you install it once, from go.dev, and type go run … in a terminal. Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Immediate mode A way of making interfaces: every moment the program describes the whole screen again from its data, so the screen can never show something out of date. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. 🚧 Not done yet Text does not wrap, except in a box with Wrap ; there is one typeface, so no monospaced table column ( layout , tables ). On the desktop: notifications, films ( ErrVideoUnsupported ) and the system's dark theme ( Android ). In a browser: only Chromium on macOS was tried; other browsers, phones and tablets, and the on-screen keyboard are not ( web ). On Android: rotating the screen, other phones and tablets, the bars' icons following the program's theme, two fingers, and shadows, sky and waves in the scene ( Android ). The family Go UI is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI (this one) buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

platforms/3ds.title: 🎮 On the Nintendo 3DS

sections.text: Writing an interface for the console

platforms/3ds.text: 🎮 On the Nintendo 3DS Status: a first step (October 2026). Built with a TinyGo that has a nintendo3ds target, a go-ui program runs on the console as homebrew, from the Homebrew Launcher: window.Run opens the console's two screens, drawn through go-renderer's nintendo3ds (citro3d). A large program (a 3D scene above, an interface of its own below) runs on a New 3DS XL at full speed; the same drawing, with a loop of its own, runs in go-3ds's explorer. Two screens Usual After SELECT Top screen (400 × 240, in 3D with the slider) The scene ( Options.Scene ) The interface, to be read Bottom screen (320 × 240, touch) The interface: the touch screen is the pointer The scene, which the finger turns and picks in A program written for a phone works unchanged: the interface is laid out for the screen it is on (320 or 400 pixels wide), and the scene gets the input the interface did not claim. With the screens swapped the interface only gets the keys, since the top screen cannot be touched. START ends the program. Button Is Cross The arrow keys L, R Minus and plus (closer and farther, for most cameras) A, B Enter and Escape; B is also the system's back Touch screen The pointer: dragging is dragging with a mouse Circle pad The stick ( input.State.Stick ): go-renderer's cameras move with it The interface may claim the keys a button stands for (A is Enter). A program that wants a button whatever the interface does reads window.ButtonsPressed() : the buttons pressed this frame, X, Y, ZL and ZR among them. What the console has not Notify , Share , OpenLink , Feel and the rest do nothing, and SystemPrefersDark is false. Preferences last only the run: TinyGo's os cannot reach the SD card yet. Films do not play. How it runs window/nintendo3ds.go reads the controls into the input state each frame ( nintendo3ds.Controls ), builds the interface, asks the program for its scene, and draws both in one frame: SceneRenderer.PaintStereo (or PaintOn the bottom screen) and FlatRenderer.PaintOn . It draws every frame, as fast as the screen shows them, and yields to the program's other goroutines after each: TinyGo's scheduler there is cooperative, and waiting for the screen happens in C. Writing an interface for the console What a phone shrugs off costs here: the processor is slower, and TinyGo's collector stops the program while it runs. These are what made the difference in a large program. Measure by phase. window.LastFrameTimes() tells how long the last frame waited for the GPU, painted the scene, painted what is drawn over it, painted the interface, and handed over. Show them in the program (a resources screen) and read them on the console: the emulator draws in software and its times are not the console's. An interface that stands still is free. go-renderer draws a list that did not change from the frame before without laying it out. Figures that change every second make their screen be laid out again each time; nothing changing every frame keeps it at almost nothing. Make the theme once. A theme (a Material one especially) is a kilobyte; keep it in a variable instead of making it in the build function. Closures capture onto the heap. Every func() { … } given to Box , Frame or Clickable that uses a variable puts that variable on the heap, every frame. Capture the few fields needed rather than a large struct (a whole report), keep the closure's work small, and keep what a frame looks up (a map of states, the texts already formatted) in the program's state, filled again with clear rather than made anew. Labels and figures. strings.ToUpper , strconv and time.Format make a string each call: keep the texts written while what they show does not change. Game looks. Look.Backdrop draws a box's background itself (pixel-art windows, keys with a lip that sinks when pressed) and TextStyle.Shadow gives text the hard shadow of a game's. Point every look at one kept value of the backdrop. Pixel fonts are crisp only at their own sizes (VT323 at 16, Silkscreen and Press Start 2P at 8 or 16), and positions should fall on whole pixels. 320 × 240 is small. Touch targets of at least 24 pixels, one line of text per row, figures large, and the buttons' hints on screen: a game's habits read well here. Building tinygo build -target=nintendo3ds -o program.3dsx ./cmd/program Copy the .3dsx to /3ds/ on the SD card. A program that reads much data at start should keep it small: the console has about 86 MB for Go, and TinyGo's collector neither moves what it keeps nor knows which words on a stack are pointers, so garbage costs more there than on a phone.

platforms/android.title: 📱 Go UI on Android

sections.text: What was checked, and what was not

platforms/android.text: 📱 Go UI on Android Status: a first step (October 2026). A Go UI program opens and draws on an Android 16 emulator, with a 3D scene under its interface, and reacts to taps and drags; the same code runs on the desktop and in a browser. The example looks like Android's own apps (Material Design 3). This page started as a plan (what to build, install and try, in which order); What was built says how it turned out, and Next what is left. What was built your program build(context) every frame: the same code as on the desktop go-ui unchanged: context, layout, controls, theme go-ui/window (android) window.Run: the interface, and a scene under it, over go-renderer's android go-renderer/android the activity, its window and touches, a thread that draws, direct OpenGL ES go-renderer/gles FlatRenderer and SceneRenderer, shared with the browser Android its own NativeActivity loads the program, a shared library built with the NDK Piece Where The window: renderers made again with each new graphics context, the insets for the interface window/android.go The activity, the drawing thread, touches, JNI for the bars and the theme, crash reports Go Renderer's android package ( its docs ) A 3D scene under the interface ( Options.Scene ), on every platform window/window.go and each platform's file An example that looks like an Android app, the same on desktop, web and Android cmd/mobile Building an installable package, with a window theme cmd/mobile/build-apk.sh , cmd/mobile/android/ There is no Java and no golang.org/x/mobile. The first step used x/mobile (gomobile); its way of calling OpenGL (every call to another thread, three at a time) was about two thirds of what a 3D view cost on a phone, and Go Renderer's own activity halved it (see A cap on frames ). Touch. The first finger down is the pointer: it moves the cursor and presses the left button, lifting it releases the button, so every control works unchanged. Other fingers are ignored until it lifts. Positions are divided by the screen's density, so layout pixels are Android's density-independent pixels (1/160 inch) and an interface is the same size on every phone. Drawing on demand. As on the desktop and in the browser, the window draws only when something happens: a touch, a size change, a frame a control asks for ( RequestFrame ) or window.Wake . A frame that would look like the one shown is not drawn. Idle on a phone, the program uses nothing at all: the drawing thread sleeps until a touch or a frame asked for. A cap on frames. Phones refresh at 90 or 120 Hz, and a finger dragging a 3D view asks for a frame at every touch event (over a hundred a second). The window draws at most Options.MaxFramesPerSecond frames a second, 60 on a phone by default; the system's own repaints do not count. Measured on a Pixel 6 Pro dragging the example's island for 10 seconds: well over a core at first (an independent measurement found 125–128 % at about 100 frames a second); 82 % with the cap and lighter frames, still through x/mobile; 41 % with Go Renderer's own activity and direct OpenGL calls. The system's bars. The window covers the whole screen, under see-through bars, as Android's own apps do. Context.Insets() says how much of each edge the status bar and the gesture bar cover, in layout pixels, so a program paints its own bars' backgrounds under them and keeps its controls clear. The window asks Android through JNI ( getRootWindowInsets ); before the window is shown it falls back on the bars' standard heights. The window theme in cmd/mobile/android/res makes the bars see-through, with dark icons in the system's light theme and light ones in its dark theme. When it closes on a phone nobody can reach. On Android the window keeps the report of a crash (an unrecovered panic, a fatal error or signal, with the failing goroutine's stack) in the application's own folder, through runtime/debug.SetCrashOutput , and window.LastCrash() gives it to the next run; window.Graphics() names the phone's OpenGL ES and GPU, or the error that stopped the window drawing. cmd/mobile shows both in its settings, and warns on its first screen after a crash, so a screenshot is enough to know what happened. The dark theme. window.SystemPrefersDark() tells whether the phone (or the browser) is set to a dark theme, so a program can follow it; cmd/mobile asks at every frame until a theme is chosen in its settings. Typing and notifications. While a text field is typed in ( Context.Typing ), the window brings the phone's on-screen keyboard up, and puts it away after. The keyboard edits the field's text, as on the phone's own fields: it suggests words from it, underlines the word it is composing, and its suggestion replaces that word ( Context.TypedField , Context.EditTypedField ). window.Notify shows a notification in the phone's shade (in a browser, through the page's notifications), once window.NotificationsAllowed ; window.AskForNotifications asks the person. On the desktop they are not shown yet. window.OpenLink(link) opens a link in the application that shows it, window.Share(title, text) offers a text through the system's sheet, Context.Copy and Context.ClipboardText reach the phone's clipboard, and window.Preference / window.KeepPreference keep small values between runs (a JSON file in the application's folder; on the desktop, the user's configuration folder; in a browser, local storage). Options.Hidden is called when the program leaves the screen, the moment to keep them, since Android may end the program after that; Options.Shown is called when it comes back (in a browser, when the page shows again), the moment to play again what Hidden stopped, such as a sound. The person's text size reaches every text through Context.SetTextScale , which the window sets in every frame. window.OpenVideo(film) plays a film's pictures (not yet its sound) in a draw2d.Image that Context.Image draws: Play , Pause , Loop , and Update in every frame it shows. On Android the phone's decoders read it; in a browser, a video element the page never shows; on the desktop it is ErrVideoUnsupported for now. window.FeelLongPress gives the short buzz of a long press ( Context.LongPressed ), where the person has touch feedback on; in a browser it vibrates where the browser can. window.Feel gives the other buzzes a phone's applications give: FeelingTick when something is chosen, FeelingConfirm when something went through, FeelingReject when something went wrong or needs a look. The wallpaper's colours. Android 12 and later make five palettes from the wallpaper (Material You), and the system's own applications take their colours from them. window.SystemPalettes() returns them, thirteen shades each, from white to black ( window.PaletteTones ), and false on an older phone, on the desktop and in a browser. They change with the wallpaper, so read them at every frame. Go UI for Android's material.System builds a Material scheme from them. A scene under the interface. Options.Scene returns, at every step, a scene and a camera to draw behind the interface, or nil for none. It gets the input the interface did not claim, so a drag on an empty part of the screen turns the camera while a drag on a slider moves the slider. The scene is drawn by Go Renderer's gles.SceneRenderer on Android and in browsers, and its OpenGL scene renderer on the desktop. cmd/mobile is built the way Android's own apps look, out of Go UI boxes, texts and clickables ( material.go ): a top app bar and a navigation bar painted under the system's bars, list items with a round icon and a Material switch, filter chips, pill-shaped buttons, cards and floating buttons, in Material Design 3's baseline colours, light and dark, and in Roboto, Android's typeface (embedded under the SIL Open Font License, in cmd/mobile/fonts , and given to the window as Options.Fonts ). Its three destinations are a list of lighthouses with their details, a map with the 3D island (drag to turn, buttons to come closer, a slider for the time of day) and settings (the dark theme, the screen's size and insets). The same program on the desktop, at a phone's size ( go run ./cmd/mobile -width 400 -height 860 ): Screen readers TalkBack reads a Go UI program as it reads Android's own applications: a finger moved over the screen reads what is under it, a swipe goes to the next thing, a double tap presses it, and the thing read is ringed. Every frame, while a screen reader is on, the interface makes its list of nodes ( screen readers ); window/android.go numbers them as Android's virtual views, says what Android widget each reads as (a switch is an android.widget.Switch ) and hands them to Go Renderer, which sends them to one small Java class only when they change. What TalkBack asks (press, long press, scroll, the thing it is on) comes back the same way. A package needs that class: go-ui-apk in Go UI for Android compiles it in. A package made without it ( cmd/mobile/build-apk.sh , which carries no Java) runs as before, without a screen reader. Building and trying it export ANDROID_HOME=…/android-sdk ANDROID_NDK_HOME=$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/<version> cmd/mobile/build-apk.sh mobile.apk adb install -r mobile.apk adb shell am start -n io.github.akrck02.goui.mobile/android.app.NativeActivity adb exec-out screencap -p > screen.png # what the screen shows adb shell input tap 230 330 # a tap, in screen pixels build-apk.sh builds the program as a shared library with the NDK's compiler (aligned to 16 KB pages, which newer phones need), and packs it with the Android SDK's tools ( aapt2 , zipalign , apksigner ) under cmd/mobile/android/AndroidManifest.xml : Android's own NativeActivity , no Java code. It signs with the debug key: for trying, not for publishing. Installed for this: the NDK (r29) through sdkmanager . The SDK, its build tools, the emulator and an arm64 Android 16 image were already there. What was checked, and what was not On the emulator (Android 16, arm64, 1080 × 2400 at 420 dots per inch): the window draws with sharp text at a density of 2.625, clear of the status bar and the gesture bar (49 and 24 layout pixels); a tap on a row opens its details and a tap on its switch flips it without opening it; the back arrow, the chips, the buttons, the navigation bar and the sliders work; the island draws at any time of day, turns with a drag and comes closer with the buttons; the dark theme switches every screen. Idle, the program uses about 0.5 % of a core; the map takes 16 draw calls a frame. On a phone (Pixel 6 Pro, Android 16, Mali-G78, 1080 × 2340): the same, in the system's dark theme at start, and after going to the background and back. That phone gives an OpenGL ES 3.2 context (first asked for version 2, through x/mobile). It found two faults the emulator hid, now fixed: the 3D map lost its ground after coming back from the background (meshes kept the buffers of the destroyed graphics context), and the program read the system's theme before Android gave it. Not yet: rotating the screen, and how it feels on other phones and tablets. Next # What Why 1 The bars' icons follow the program's theme , not only the system's: a JNI call on Android's interface thread Dark icons on a dark app (when the app's theme differs from the phone's) 2 Material pieces in Go UI itself : a touch theme, the switch, list items, the navigation bar, now in the example Every program gets them, not only the example 3 The on-screen keyboard Done: it comes up while a field is typed in ( Context.Typing ) 4 Long press , two fingers, the back gesture Long press done ( Context.LongPressed ); pinch to zoom the map, back from a lighthouse's details 5 Shadows, sky and waves on phones, as on the desktop The scene is Go Renderer's simple one on phones and in browsers Risks Phones differ. The window was tried on a Mali GPU (Pixel 6 Pro) and the emulator; an Adreno phone closed the first version, for a reason not known yet (the crash report will tell). Battery : drawing on demand is a must on a phone, and it is in place, with a cap of 60 frames a second.

platforms/web.title: 🌐 In a web browser

sections.text: How the window works in a page
What was checked, and what was not

platforms/web.text: 🌐 In a web browser Status: a first step (October 2026). Go UI applications run in a browser, built for WebAssembly and drawn through WebGL2, with the same code as on the desktop. The desktop is unchanged. The register above is cmd/app , not changed by a line : window.Run opens a canvas instead of a window when the program is built for the browser. GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build -o web/app.wasm ./cmd/app cp "$(go env GOROOT)/lib/wasm/wasm_exec.js" web/ python3 -m http.server -d web 8080 # then open http://localhost:8080/?program=app web/index.html is one page for every program: ?program=name runs name.wasm from the same folder. Over a 3D scene cmd/web is the same kind of program as cmd/example : the lighthouse island with a panel to look after its light and a status bar. On the desktop, viewer.Run draws the scene; it needs GLFW, so in a browser the program puts the pieces together itself, in about thirty lines: canvas, _ := browser.OpenCanvas("view") functions, _ := canvas.WebGL(true) // antialiased, for the 3D edges renderer, _ := gles.NewSceneRenderer(functions, overlay.Fonts{}) world.Overlay.Drawing = interfaceContext.Drawing() app.Update = func(app *rendererwindow.Application, step float64) error { interfaceContext.Begin(app.Input) lighthousePanel(interfaceContext, light) interfaceContext.End() unclaimed := app.Input.Unclaimed() // the camera gets what the panel did not take orbit.Update(&unclaimed, step, &app.Camera) return nil } browser.Run(canvas, app, func() error { renderer.Draw(world, app.Camera, width, height) return nil }) GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build -o web/web.wasm ./cmd/web # then ?program=web The scene is drawn by Go Renderer's simple OpenGL ES renderer: light, fog and water, but no shadows or sky yet (see Go Renderer's docs/web.md ). How the window works in a page On the desktop In a browser A GLFW window, sized by Options.Width and Height The page's canvas ( Options.Canvas , its id; the first canvas when empty), sized by the page Metal or OpenGL 4.1 WebGL2, through Go Renderer's gles.FlatRenderer : the same atlas and quads, one draw call Options.Title is the window's title It becomes the page's title Sleeps in glfw.WaitEvents between frames Asks for an animation frame only when something happens window.Wake() posts an empty event window.Wake() asks for an animation frame Closing the window ends Run window.Stop() ends Run , for a page that takes the canvas away (below) Everything else is shared: one interface step per frame, no frame when the draw list's fingerprint says it would look the same, Options.Continuous to draw every frame. Measured in the register: no frames at all in two seconds of idling . One screen of a larger web application. Give the program the page's canvas by id ( Options.Canvas ) and leave Options.Title empty, so the page keeps its own title. When the page leaves that screen, it asks the program to stop (a function the program hands the page through syscall/js calls window.Stop() ): Run returns, the canvas's listeners come off the page and the program exits. Opening the screen again starts a new one. The window's code is split by build tags: window.go (options, the interface application, frames that look the same) for everyone, desktop.go , thread.go and the Metal files for desktops, and web.go for WebAssembly. Text, keys and the clipboard Keys arrive by their place on the keyboard, as on the desktop, and typed characters as the browser gives them, so accents and other layouts work. Copy (Cmd or Ctrl and C) offers the text to the system clipboard too; paste takes what the browser's paste event brings. What was checked, and what was not Checked in Chromium on macOS: the register (filters, selecting rows, the inspector), the scene example (buttons, a checkbox, a slider, typing and deleting in a text field, turning the camera around the panel), sharp text on a high-density screen, and no frames while idle. Not yet: other browsers, phones and tablets (touch arrives as a pointer, but Go UI has no touch theme yet), the on-screen keyboard, and very large tables (each frame copies the draw list into JavaScript once, which should be fine). Size A program is one .wasm file of about 5.8 MB, about 1.9 MB compressed (web servers usually compress on the fly). The fonts and icons are inside; the page loads nothing else.

project/performance-audit.title: ⚡ Performance and battery audit
project/performance-audit.text: ⚡ Performance and battery audit Date: October 2026. Scope: Go UI and the 2D path of Go Renderer it draws through (draw list, painter, atlas, flat renderer, window loop), measured with the register application ( cmd/app ). Machine: a laptop with an Apple M4 and a 60 Hz built-in screen, macOS 26, Go 1.25. The short answer: an idle application now costs nothing , and a frame of a normal interface is cheap. What is left to win is work done in frames that change nothing, and work that grows with content nobody sees (rows scrolled out of view). A Metal backend was not needed for battery, but once built it turned out cheaper than OpenGL on macOS, above all in memory ( Metal ). How it was measured The whole program , in a real window at 1280 × 720: processor time ( ps ), idle wakeups and energy ( top -stats cpu,idlew,power ), GPU use ( ioreg , "Device Utilization %"), memory ( footprint ), frames per second (a probe program counting frames). One frame , without a window: Go benchmarks with the real fonts at a 2560 × 1440 framebuffer, CPU and allocation profiles ( go test -bench -cpuprofile -memprofile , go tool pprof ). The benchmark files stay in the repositories so the numbers can be measured again: File What it measures go-ui/cmd/app/audit_bench_test.go A frame of the register: idle, pointer moving, a field focused, typing, a search, 11 to 3000 rows; the painter on that frame go-ui/audit_frame_test.go Struct sizes, ScrollArea against List from 11 to 10 000 rows, the phases of a frame, the text field, cache misses go-ui/audit_render_test.go The update step, painting, the whole frame's CPU, hashing the draw list, whether an idle pointer move changes it go-renderer/opengl/overlay/audit_painter_test.go The painter on 2000 commands, vertex filling (now and packed), sorting, clipping, glyphs, shadows, atlas growth go-renderer/opengl/overlay/audit_register_paint_test.go The painter on the register's draw list, per text line and per character go test ./cmd/app -run Audit -bench Audit -benchmem go test . -run Audit -bench Audit -benchmem The whole program Register at 1280 × 720 Draws on demand (default) Draws every frame ( -continuous ) Processor, idle 0.14 % (0.10 s in 60 s) 3.9 % (2.45 s in 60 s) GPU, idle 0 % 16 % Idle wakeups 0 0 Frames while idle 0 (6 at start-up) 60 to 120 per second, for 60 updates Memory (system footprint) 116 MB 166 MB Memory was 186 MB before this audit: the window asked for a depth and stencil buffer that flat drawing never uses. FlatOnly now leaves it out. Of what remains, about 70 MB is the window's own buffers that macOS keeps (they grow with the window) and about 25 MB the program itself. One frame Frame Go UI (build, layout, draw list) Painter (draw list to quads) Vertex filling OpenGL calls Register, 11 rows 44 µs, 114 allocations 85 µs 13 µs about 0.1–0.2 ms Register, 1000 rows 1.9 ms, 4077 allocations 3.65 ms 13 µs the same Register, 1000 rows in a List 77 µs, 65 allocations about 0.1 ms 13 µs the same Hovering, typing and a focused field cost about the same as an idle frame. At 120 pointer events a second, the 11-row register spends about 1.7 % of a core; with 1000 rows in a ScrollArea , about 67 %, and from about 2000 rows it no longer fits in a frame. Findings Ranked by what they cost the battery. Effort: S under half a day, M one or two days, L more. # Finding Where Impact Fix Effort 1 Frames that change nothing are painted and shown. A pointer moving over still areas, the frame that follows input, and in continuous mode up to half of all frames (60 to 120 shown for 60 updates) produce a draw list identical to the last opengl/opengl.go loop, waitForWork High: each is a full paint, upload, draw and swap Hash the draw list (6 µs) with the background, size and scale; when unchanged, skip painting, drawing and the swap. In continuous mode, draw only after an update step S–M 2 Rows out of sight are built, laid out and painted. A table in a ScrollArea costs 1.9 µs per row whether seen or not go-ui/scroll.go , paint.go ; cmd/app table High for long lists: 25 to 47 times less with List Use List for long tables (the example should); in paintBox , skip children outside the clip S (app), M (library) 3 Text cut away by a clip is laid out glyph by glyph, then thrown away. 29 % of the quads of a scrolled panel, 98 % at 1000 rows draw2d/list.go (texts are never culled), overlay/drawing.go High for long lists: 3.65 ms to about 0.1 ms at 1000 rows Reject a text whose line (baseline minus size to baseline plus a third) misses the clip, before laying it out S 4 The text measure cache empties itself when full , in the middle of a frame, past 4096 texts go-ui/paint.go Medium: +37 % frame time from 1900 to 2100 rows Keep two generations, so texts used this frame are never dropped S 5 Each character is looked up twice , with a []rune conversion per text overlay/layout.go ( drawable , hasGlyph ), overlay/drawing.go Medium: 64 ns per character, 62 % of painting One atlas lookup that also knows a missing glyph; a direct table for ASCII M 6 192 bytes per quad, in a buffer reallocated every frame (0.5–1.2 MB a frame) opengl/overlay.go Medium in continuous mode Instanced quads of about 32 bytes; keep the buffer and use BufferSubData M 7 Rendering at the display rate is not guaranteed by vsync on macOS: 60, 90 and 120 fps were measured on a 60 Hz screen, even with SwapInterval(1) (now set explicitly) opengl/window.go Medium in continuous mode Finding 1 caps it: no update, no frame S 8 Large structs copied by value : an element is 344 bytes, a draw command 136; copying is about 20 % of a frame go-ui/element.go , layout.go , draw2d/list.go Low to medium, grows with the tree Build elements in place; smaller enums; cold fields apart M 9 The whole atlas is uploaded again when one glyph or corner is added (1 MB, 16 MB at its largest), and nothing is ever evicted opengl/overlay.go , overlay/atlas.go Low: one-off pauses, not steady cost Upload only the changed rectangle ( TexSubImage2D ) S 10 The flat path does 3D work : a second full-screen clear, the 3D program bound, the 3D shaders compiled at start opengl/opengl.go Low When FlatOnly , let the flat renderer own the frame S 11 A dual-GPU Intel Mac stays on the discrete GPU while an OpenGL window is open: GLFW does not opt into graphics switching by default opengl/window.go High on those Macs, none on Apple silicon glfw.WindowHint(glfw.CocoaGraphicsSwitching, glfw.True) for flat windows S 12 The caret wakes the window twice a second for as long as a field has the focus go-ui/textfield.go Low Stop blinking after a while without typing, as macOS does S 13 A focused field measures prefixes every frame , needed only while clicking or dragging go-ui/textfield.go Low (16 allocations a frame with a long text) Measure only on press or drag; keep widths until the text or caret changes S 14 The example application allocates every frame : the dark theme built twice to compare it, fmt per cell, the order sorted and the search lower-cased three times per row cmd/app Low, but it is the code people copy Keep themes in variables; work out the shown rows once; make ParseHex allocation-free S 15 Small per-frame bookkeeping : the painter sorts commands that are already in order; rootElementOf walks up for every element; memory maps are scanned every frame several Very low Check before sorting; record the root while building; sweep every 60 frames S 16 StartLoop crashes when not called on the main thread (macOS needs it), and says nothing about it opengl/opengl.go Robustness, not speed Document it and check it at start S Measured and found fine: one draw call and one program per frame, uniform locations cached, no glGetError , cursor shape and lock changed only when they change, the window title updated only in continuous mode, no busy waiting when idle, theme changes and window resizes do not rasterise glyphs again. A partial redraw (repainting only what changed) is not worth it: after a swap the back buffer is undefined on macOS, so it would need a full copy each frame. Done: steps 1 to 4 Applied in October 2026, with tests for each; the documentation captures came out identical, pixel for pixel. Measured again Before After Register frame, 11 rows (Go UI) 44 µs, 114 allocations 37 µs, 109 allocations Register frame, 1000 rows (Go UI) 1.9 ms 55 µs Register frame, 3000 rows (Go UI) 7.5 ms 109 µs Painter, register with 1000 rows 3.65 ms 69 µs Continuous mode, frames shown 60 to 120 a second 60, one per update, and none when nothing changed Continuous mode, GPU 16 % 0 % while nothing changes Memory (system footprint) 116 MB 93 MB What changed: Frames that would look the same are skipped (1, 7). draw2d.List.Fingerprint sums up a draw list; Go UI's window answers Go Renderer's new Application.Unchanged with it, and the loop then neither draws nor presents. In continuous mode a frame is drawn only after an update step, and the loop sleeps until the next one. What is out of sight costs nothing (2, 3). The draw list drops texts whose line misses the clip; Go UI does not paint elements wholly outside a clipping box; the example's table is a List , and works out its rows once a frame. The text cache keeps two generations (4), and a focused field measures only when something changed (13), keeps its text as a string, and stops blinking after ten seconds without a key or a click (12). The flat window is flat (10, 11, 16): no 3D shaders, matrices or second clear; automatic graphics switching on Macs with two GPUs; StartLoop returns an error off the main thread instead of crashing. What to do, in order Skip unchanged frames (finding 1), with continuous mode drawing only after an update (7). Stop paying for what is out of sight : cull texts by the clip in the painter (3), skip children outside the clip in Go UI (2), and move the example's table to List . The text cache's generations (4) and the field's measuring (13). Graphics switching for flat windows (11) and the flat path's own frame (10). The painter's per-character work (5), packed instanced quads (6) and partial atlas uploads (9). Smaller items: copies (8), the caret (12), the example (14), bookkeeping (15), the main thread (16). Steps 1 to 4 are done (above); step 5 and the smaller items are left. Metal Built after this audit, as insurance against OpenGL leaving macOS: Go UI's window now draws through Metal on macOS ( -backend opengl goes back). It costs less than OpenGL, which on macOS runs on a translation layer over Metal: OpenGL Metal Register idle, memory 93–102 MB 66–70 MB Changing every frame: processor 13.6 % of a core 9 % Changing every frame: GPU 19–20 % 12–16 % Changing every frame: memory 163 MB 107 MB Still again, memory 109 MB 60 MB The details, and what still needs a look on screen, are in Go Renderer's docs/metal.md . Keyboard focus Measured when Tab learned to reach every control ( proposal 1 ), on a Linux container with 8 cores and Go 1.26, not the M4 above: compare the rows with each other, not with the tables before. BenchmarkThreeHundredControls , six runs Time per frame Allocations Before 161.2–162.2 µs 162 (2763 B) After, the default WhenGiven (no keyboard) 162.6–164.3 µs 162 (2763 B) After, Always with a button focused ( …WithTheKeyboard ) 163.4–165.2 µs 162 (2763 B) A frame does no new allocation, which TestAFrameWithFocusAllocatesNothingMore checks. The time grows by 1 to 2 %, from the one comparison every control makes (is it the focused one, is it held?) and, while the interface has the keyboard, from adding each control to the Tab order. The ring is one stroke, and the press rescales the commands of one control while it is held.

proposals/driving-an-interface.title: 3. Driving an interface: automatic modes, and tests on the device
proposals/driving-an-interface.text: 3. Driving an interface: automatic modes, and tests on the device Status: done · Author's approval: proposal ☑ (2026-10-21, "sigue, hazlo") plan ☑ (2026-10-21, the same words: the author asked to go ahead without stopping) Why uitest drives an interface with no display: it finds what was drawn by its name ("Add an action", "Pad A") and gives it input, frame by frame, on a clock of its own. That idea is useful far beyond go test , but today it only works in a test window. A real Go UI window, on a computer, a phone or a 3DS, cannot be driven: No automatic modes. A program cannot play a demo of itself (an attract mode), guide a person through a tutorial with a pointer that shows press here on the real control, or replay what someone did to reproduce a bug they reported. No tests on the device. uitest proves the interface's logic on the computer, but not what only a device does: Go UI for Android's bridge to Java, the system keyboard with its suggestions, TalkBack, the screen's insets; Go Renderer drawing on the 3DS's GPU and its buttons. Today those are checked by hand, with captures from the emulators. Two copies of one idea. If a program wrote its own driver, it would copy what uitest already does, and the two would drift apart. What Id Requirement Check R1 A window can be driven : a program gives window.Options a driver, which adds input to each frame before the interface runs (a pointer, keys, fingers, typed text), on every target: desktop, web, Android and the 3DS test with a made-up driver in a window loop; a demo run on each target R2 A script says what to do, by the names people see: move to, click, tap, hold, drag, type, press a key, wait, wait until an element shows; each step finds its element in the live interface as uitest does tests of each step against a made-up interface R3 uitest runs the same scripts and shares the code that finds elements and makes input: one implementation, two places to run it uitest 's tests pass unchanged; no finding code left in two packages R4 A script can be recorded from what a person does in a window, and saved as a file a person can read and edit; played back, it does the same test: record a session, play it back, the interface ends in the same state R5 A driven window can show what the driver does: the pointer, the fingers, the element a step found, so a demo or a tutorial is seen, not only run capture of a tutorial step R6 A script run on a device reports each step's result with the error codes uitest uses, as lines a test runner reads (Android's log, the 3DS's console, standard output) test of the report's format; a script run in the Android emulator and in Azahar R7 Go UI for Android gains a test that installs an app in the emulator, runs a script on it and reads the report, so its own layer (the Java bridge, the keyboard, TalkBack's tree, the insets) is proven automatically the test passes in the emulator R8 A window with no driver costs nothing: no allocation and no work each frame; programs that do not use it are unchanged benchmark of the window loop with and without; the samples unchanged R9 A person always wins: any real input while a script plays stops it, so an automatic mode never fights the hand on the device test: a key pressed during a script stops it Out of scope Automating other programs or the operating system (UIAutomator, accessibility services): this drives Go UI's own windows only. Comparing pictures pixel by pixel: it needs Go Renderer to paint with no display, which is its own proposal. Driving a window from another computer over the network. A script language with branches and loops: a script is a list of steps; a program that needs logic writes Go. Decided questions The script file's format: a line per step , plain text a person reads and writes, with # comments. Each line is parsed into a step; an error names its line. The shared code lives in a new package, uidrive : it finds elements by name in the live interface, makes input for a step, and runs a script frame by frame on a clock. uitest is rebuilt on it. R7 lives in Go UI for Android , which owns the layer it proves. It is a later task there, not part of this change (see Tasks). Design A driver is a hook in the window loop. uidrive.Driver is an interface of two methods: Drive(state, context) runs after the backend gathered the frame's real input and before the interface's Begin , and adds input to the state; Show(drawing) runs after End , and may draw over the interface. window.Options.Driver takes one. Desktop, web and Android share interfaceApplication 's Update , and the 3DS has its own consoleRun.step : both call the same two lines, behind if driver != nil , so a window without one does what it did (R1, R8). uidrive (new package, pure Go, so it builds for TinyGo and WebAssembly): File What it holds errors.go Code , Error , CodeOf ; the element codes moved from uitest , which keep their stable names ( uitest.element-not-found …) since programs and people check them; new uidrive.script-not-read (with the line) and uidrive.script-stopped find.go Element , Find , FindIn , FindWithin , FindAt , Texts : what uitest/find.go did, over a *ui.Context (its screen reader's nodes and its drawing) hand.go Hand : the pointer, the fingers and typing made as input on an input.State (move, press, release, touch, type, keys, let go of all) script.go , parse.go , keys.go Script , Step , Action ; Parse reads the line format and Script.String writes it; the keys' names player.go , plan.go Player : runs a script one frame at a time on the state's clock; a Driver . plan turns a step into its moves, a frame each report.go one line per step, uidrive: step 3 failed uitest.element-not-found: click "Remove" , to an io.Writer the program gives recorder.go Recorder : a Driver that adds nothing and writes down what a person does, as a Script show.go the overlay: the pointer, the fingers and the element found, drawn by Player.Show when asked uitest keeps its whole API. Element , Error and Code become aliases of uidrive 's; its finders call uidrive.Find… ; its pointer, touches and keys go through a uidrive.Hand . It gains a Driver option (the window calls it each frame, as a real one) and Window.Play(script) , which runs a script with a sixtieth of a second per frame on the test clock (R3). ui.Context gains Measurer() , which finding a text needs. On Android the window keeps the screen reader's nodes on while driven, since a driver finds elements through them. The script format , one step per line: # a lighthouse keeper writes the day's log click "Add an entry" type "Fog at dawn" press Enter wait 0.5s until "Saved" # waits up to 5s, or: until "Saved" 10s tap "Light the lamp" hold "Lens" 1s # a long press drag "Boat" 120 0 # by a distance in layout pixels; or: drag "Boat" to "Harbour" scroll "Log" -3 double-click "Entry" move-to "Help" click-at 40 300 # a place, when what is there has no name press Shift+Tab The person wins (R9): a Player that finds input in the state before adding its own ( input.State.HasInput ) stops, lets go of what it holds, and ends with uidrive.script-stopped . Alternatives not taken. JSON scripts: diffable, but noisy to write by hand. Keeping the finding code in uitest and importing it from windows: uitest imports testing , which has no place in a program on a console. A driver as a func : an interface lets one value both drive and show, and a nil check costs the same. A second, input-replaying recorder (raw events with times): it would break when the layout moves; names survive a new layout. Tasks [x] T1 — move finding into uidrive ( Element , Find… , errors); ui.Context.Measurer ; uitest finds through it · uidrive/errors.go , uidrive/find.go , ui.go , uitest/find.go , uitest/errors.go · serves R3 · test: TestAButtonIsFoundByItsLabelInTheLiveInterface , and uitest 's tests unchanged [x] T2 — uidrive.Hand makes the pointer, touch and key input; uitest acts through it · uidrive/hand.go , uitest/pointer.go , uitest/touch.go , uitest/keyboard.go · serves R3 · test: TestTheFirstFingerDownAlsoPressesThePointer [x] T3 — the script format: Parse and Script.String · uidrive/script.go · serves R2 · test: TestAScriptWrittenAndReadAgainIsTheSame , TestAnUnknownStepIsAnErrorWithItsLine [x] T4 — Player runs each step frame by frame; uitest.Driver and Window.Play · uidrive/ player.go , uitest/window.go , uitest/play.go · serves R2, R3 · test: one per step against a made-up interface ( TestAClickStepPressesTheButtonByItsName …) [x] T5 — the report, a line per step with its code · uidrive/report.go · serves R6 · test: TestTheReportSaysEachStepAndTheCodeOfAFailure [x] T6 — a person's input stops a script · uidrive/player.go · serves R9 · test: TestAKeyPressedDuringAScriptStopsIt [x] T7 — window.Options.Driver on every target, at no cost without one · window/window.go , window/nintendo3ds.go , window/android.go , window/drive.go · serves R1, R8 · test: TestADriverAddsInputBeforeTheInterfaceRuns , TestAWindowWithoutADriverAllocatesNothingForIt , BenchmarkAWindowStep… ; guide page docs/4-guides/12-driving-a-window.md [x] T8 — Recorder writes down a person's session as a script · uidrive/recorder.go · serves R4 · test: TestARecordedSessionPlayedBackEndsInTheSameState [x] T9 — the overlay: pointer, fingers and the element found · uidrive/show.go , cmd/app (its -script and -record flags: cmd/example draws through go-renderer's viewer, not a window) · serves R5 · test: TestAShownPlayerDrawsThePointerAndTheElementItFound ; a capture [ ] Later, in go-ui-android (not this change) — R7: a test that installs an application in the emulator, plays a script on it with its report going to Android's log, and reads the log for uidrive: script passed Result Built (branch feature/driving-an-interface , written with an AI assistant and pending the author's review): uidrive , a new package: finding by name ( Find , FindIn , FindWithin , FindAt …), a Hand that makes pointer, touch and key input, the line script format ( Parse , Script.String ), a Player with its report and its overlay, and a Recorder . uitest rebuilt on it, with its API and its tests' behaviour unchanged (R3). The only test that changed is TestEachErrorCarriesItsCode : the element errors' constructors moved to uidrive , whose own test checks them. uitest gains Driver and Window.Play . window.Options.Driver , called in interfaceApplication (desktop, web, Android) and in the 3DS's consoleRun.step ; on Android the screen reader's nodes stay on while driven (R1). ui.Context.Measurer , which finding a line of text needs. cmd/app -script and -record ; the guide docs/4-guides/12-driving-a-window.md , a section in the testing guide, and the reference regenerated. Checks run: Id How it was checked R1 TestADriverAddsInputBeforeTheInterfaceRuns ; on the desktop, cmd/app -script played a script on Xvfb; the web build ( GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build ./window ./uidrive ./cmd/web ) and a driven program for the 3DS ( tinygo build -target=nintendo3ds ) compile R2 a test per step in uidrive/player_test.go ; script_test.go for the format and its errors R3 every uitest test passes; finding lives only in uidrive/find.go R4 TestARecordedSessionPlayedBackEndsInTheSameState ; on the desktop, a session recorded with cmd/app -record (clicks and typing through xdotool) played back with every step passing R5 TestAShownPlayerDrawsThePointerAndTheElementItFound ; the capture docs/images/driving-a-window.png R6 TestTheReportSaysEachStepAndTheCodeOfAFailure ; the report on standard output on the desktop R8 TestAWindowWithoutADriverAllocatesNothingForIt ; BenchmarkAWindowStepWithoutADriver and …WithADriver : 0 allocations, about 475 ns a step either way R9 TestAKeyPressedDuringAScriptStopsIt ; on the desktop a real pointer move stopped a playing script with uidrive.script-stopped Not built: R7, the emulator test, which belongs to go-ui-android (see Tasks). A recording leaves out a drag that starts on something with no name. Still for a person to check: a script played on an Android phone or emulator, and on a 3DS or Azahar: neither was run here (no Android NDK to build the Android window here, and the 3DS program was built but not started), so R1 and R6 are proven by the desktop and the tests only. The Android change ( SetScreenReader(… || driven) ) was not compiled. The overlay's colours and sizes were seen on a light theme only.

proposals/keyboard-focus-and-press.title: 1. Keyboard focus on every control, and a press that gives
proposals/keyboard-focus-and-press.text: 1. Keyboard focus on every control, and a press that gives Status: done · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ Why Today the keyboard only reaches text fields: Tab goes from one field to the next, and buttons, check boxes and choices can only be used with a pointer. That breaks the first rule of an accessible interface, that the keyboard reaches everything. Bubble 4 has also settled how focus and pressing should look (focus lights the control's own edge; a control shrinks a little while pressed), and go-ui should let a design system ask for that through its theme, as it already does for colours and corners. What Id Requirement Check R1 While the interface has the keyboard, Tab and Shift+Tab move the focus through every control that can be used, fields included, in the order they are drawn test TestTabVisitsEveryControlInTheOrderItIsDrawn R2 Enter or Space presses the focused button, ticks the focused check box, picks the focused choice test TestTheKeyboardUsesTheFocusedControl R3 The focused control shows a ring only when the focus came from the keyboard, never after a click or a tap; a click sets where the next Tab goes on from test TestAClickGivesFocusWithoutARing R4 The ring lies on the control's edge; on a control filled with the primary colour it is drawn inside, in the colour of its text tests TestTheRingLiesOnTheEdge , TestTheRingOfAPrimaryButtonIsInside R5 A theme can ask a field to light its own border instead of drawing a ring around it test TestAFieldCanLightItsOwnBorder R6 A theme can ask controls to shrink a little while held; with less motion asked by the system, they don't tests TestAHeldButtonShrinks , TestLessMotionKeepsAHeldButtonStill R7 A theme made before these tokens draws exactly as before, apart from the ring that keyboard focus now shows cmd/app captures before and after, compared pixel by pixel with no keyboard focus R8 Bubble's goui adapter sets the new tokens, so a Bubble theme in go-ui behaves like Bubble's CSS test in bubble/goui ; the showcase compared with the browser R9 go-ui only takes Tab, Enter, Space and the arrows while the interface has the keyboard: a field is being typed in, a dialog, sheet or menu is open, the program gave it the keyboard, or the program says the interface is all there is. Otherwise every key reaches the program: a 3D view or a game keeps them tests TestAGameKeepsTabAndSpaceWhileTheInterfaceDoesNotHaveTheKeyboard , TestAClickOnAButtonDoesNotTakeTheKeyboard , TestTakeKeyboardGivesItAndEscapeGivesItBack , TestThePauseMenuOfTheGuideWorks R10 A frame costs the same as today: no allocation added per frame, the 300-control benchmark within 3 % of today, and a still interface still draws nothing new testing.AllocsPerRun on a frame with focus; BenchmarkThreeHundredControls before and after; the existing idle test R11 The docs explain who has the keyboard so a newcomer picks the right mode: a guide with a game or 3D view ( WhenGiven ) and a form-only app ( Always ), what a click does and does not do, how Escape and TakeKeyboard work, and a table of which keys each mode reads The guide's examples run as shown; the author reads it Out of scope Arrow keys inside lists, menus and grids: Tab reaches the list, and moving inside it is a later proposal. Changes for screen readers: they already have their own focus ( SetScreenReaderFocus ). Animating the press: it shrinks while held and comes back, with no tween, until go-ui has one. Design Who has the keyboard : the program decides, through one field on the context: KeyboardNavigation: WhenGiven (the default, chosen by the author: if a program forgets to choose, the worst case is that Tab does not walk the buttons, not that a game stops answering): the interface has the keyboard only while a field is typed in, a modal layer (dialog, sheet, menu) is open, or the program calls TakeKeyboard() . Escape, or ReleaseKeyboard() , gives it back. A click on a button does not take the keyboard, so Space in a game never presses the last button clicked. KeyboardNavigation: Always : for programs that are only an interface (a register, a settings app). Tab always moves the focus. While the interface has the keyboard, go-ui claims it in the input state, as fields do today, so go-renderer's viewer and a game's own controls know to stay quiet. Otherwise it claims nothing and reads no key. Cost : the focus order is a slice of IDs kept on the context and reset to length zero each frame, so it allocates nothing once warm; nothing is added to it while the interface does not have the keyboard. The ring is one stroke, only on the focused control. The press scales one element while it is held. Moving the focus changes the drawing, so it redraws; a still interface with no keys pressed draws nothing new, as today. Focus order : every pressable control and every field joins a list in drawing order, each frame. The tabFrom and tabBack that fields already use move over that list instead of the fields alone. The focus stays an ID , so it survives from frame to frame as it does today. Keyboard or pointer : keyboardFocus is the control Tab reached; any press of the pointer clears it, so the ring (painted only on it) shows only for focus from the keyboard, which is what CSS calls :focus-visible . A click remembers its control, and Tab goes on from it. Theme tokens , all zero for go-ui's own look: FocusWidth : the ring's width. Zero keeps today's 3 pixels. FieldFocusEdge : when true, a field colours its border with FocusRing and draws no ring. PressScale : how big a held control is drawn (0.97 in Bubble). Zero means it doesn't change. The ring of a control filled with Primary is drawn inside it in OnPrimary , always: a ring in FocusRing could not be told from the fill. Less motion : go-renderer's input state does not carry the platform's setting yet, so a LessMotion field on the context lets the program say so. Painting : the ring is one more Rectangle stroke in paint.go , from the element's rectangle and corner. The press scales the element's rectangle around its centre before painting it and its children, so text and icons shrink with it. Not taken: rings that follow the browser's look with a gap. Bubble chose an edge with no gap, and a gap only looks right on the page's own background.
