} if context.PrimaryButton("Remove") { program.remove() context.Toast(name+" was removed", false) } }) }) if dismissed { program.removing = false } } func (program *register) add() { program.added++ program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses, lighthouse{name: fmt.Sprintf("New lighthouse %d", program.added), rangeNM: 10, period: 5}) program.selected = len(program.lighthouses) - 1 program.search = "" } func (program *register) remove() { program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses[:program.selected], program.lighthouses[program.selected+1:]...) program.selected = min(program.selected, len(program.lighthouses)-1) program.removing = false } favourite.go and flashes.go are above, each with package main and its imports ( github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/draw2d and ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" ). ← Lesson 4 · Lesson 6: over a 3D scene →

the-quest/immediate-mode.title: Lesson 1: immediate mode

sections.text: Ids: how Go UI tells controls apart

the-quest/immediate-mode.text: Lesson 1: immediate mode In this lesson you write the smallest useful Go UI program, a lamp that is switched on and off, and learn the one idea everything else rests on: the interface is a function of your data, called again at every frame . Mission Pieces Time A lamp to switch on and off window.Run , controls that return what happened, ids 10 min The idea Immediate mode is a whiteboard : every frame you wipe it and draw it again from your notes (your variables). Nothing on the board can go stale, because nothing on it is kept; a button is simply drawn, and tells you if someone pressed it. A frame // The first go-ui program: a lighthouse whose lamp is switched on and off, counting the switches. package main import ( "flag" "fmt" "log" ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" "github.com/akrck02/go-ui/window" ) func main() { options := window.Options{Title: "Lighthouse"} options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) // -capture, -dark, -width, -height… flag.Parse() lit := false // the program's own data: go-ui keeps none of it switches := 0 build := func(context *ui.Context) { context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(24), Gap: 12}, func() { context.Heading("North Point") if lit { context.Label("The lamp is lit.") } else { context.Label("The lamp is dark.") } context.Caption(fmt.Sprintf("Switched %d times", switches)) label := "Switch on" if lit { label = "Switch off" } if context.PrimaryButton(label + "##switch") { lit = !lit switches++ } }) } if err := window.Run(options, build); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } The program in the light and the dark theme: a title, two lines and a button Read build from top to bottom, as Go UI does at every frame: A box that stacks its children vertically, as wide as the window, with 24 pixels of padding and 12 between children. Boxes are the only way Go UI arranges things ( lesson 2 ). A heading, then one of two lines, chosen with an ordinary if . A caption with the count, formatted from your variable. A button. PrimaryButton draws it in the theme's primary colour and returns true on the frame it is clicked : that is where you change your data. There is no OnClick , no button object, no "update the label" step. The next frame calls build again, which reads lit and switches again, and the screen follows. 📝 When is build called? Whenever something could have changed: input, a resize, a frame a control asks for (a caret's blink). In between, the window sleeps and the program uses no processor. From another goroutine (a download finished) call window.Wake() . Ids: how Go UI tells controls apart Go UI keeps a little state between frames: which control is pressed, which field has the keyboard, where a list is scrolled. It finds it again by each control's id , a hash of its label and the scopes around it. The button's label changes, "Switch on" or "Switch off", but it must stay the same button (or a press that started on one would end on another). Everything after ## is part of the id but not shown: "Switch on##switch" and "Switch off##switch" are one button. Two buttons both called "Remove" in a loop would share an id. Open a scope per item with context.Push(name) and close it with context.Pop() ; you will do it in lesson 3 . Panels open a scope with their title, so "Apply" in two panels never mixes. The text controls Call Draws Heading(text) A bold title Label(text) Body text Caption(text) Small, quiet text: hints and counts Text(text, ui.TextStyle{Size, Weight, Color}) Any size, weight ( draw2d.Regular , Medium , Bold , Mono ) and colour Icon(name) A Lucide icon by name Checkpoint A window with North Point , a line saying whether the lamp is lit, a count, and a button whose words change as you click it. Achievement unlocked: Switchman What you learnt window.Run calls your function at every frame; it describes the whole interface. Controls are function calls that return what happened; your variables hold the state. Ids come from labels and scopes; ## keeps an id while the words change. Bonus (optional) Add a second button, "Reset", that sets the count back to zero, and show it only once the lamp has been switched at least once. ← Tutorial · Lesson 2: layout →

the-quest/layout.title: Lesson 2: layout
the-quest/layout.text: Lesson 2: layout In this lesson you build the skeleton of the register: a toolbar across the top, a list down the left that can be made wider, the content in the middle and a status bar at the foot. You learn how Go UI sizes and places boxes . Mission Pieces Time The window's skeleton Box , Frame , Fit , Grow , Fixed , Resizable 15 min The idea Layout is packing a suitcase : some things have a fixed size (a book), some fit what they hold (a bag of socks), and the rest grow into whatever room is left. You say which is which; Go UI does the packing at the end of the frame. The skeleton: a toolbar, the list of lighthouses on the left, a hint in the middle, the status bar The program's data From here on the program keeps its state in a struct, and build is a method on it: // lighthouse is the program's own data: the interface shows it and changes it, and keeps none. type lighthouse struct { name string colour int // an index into colours rangeNM float32 // how far the light is seen, in nautical miles period float32 // seconds between flashes lit bool foghorn bool favourite bool } var colours = []string{"White", "Red", "Green", "Amber"} // register is everything the program remembers between frames. type register struct { lighthouses []lighthouse selected int // -1 = none search string sideWidth float32 removing bool // the sheet asking before a removal is open added int // how many were added, to name new ones } func main() { options := window.Options{Title: "Lighthouse register"} options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) flag.Parse() options.MinWidth, options.MinHeight = 640, 400 // the smallest the layout still works at program := &register{ lighthouses: []lighthouse{ {name: "North Point", rangeNM: 18, period: 5, lit: true}, {name: "East Cape", colour: 1, rangeNM: 12, period: 3, lit: true, foghorn: true}, {name: "Harbour Mole", colour: 2, rangeNM: 6, period: 2}, {name: "South Reef", colour: 3, rangeNM: 15, period: 10, lit: true}, }, sideWidth: 240, } if err := window.Run(options, program.build); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } Boxes Every control is a box, and boxes nest. A ui.Layout says how a box sizes itself and places its children: Field Means Direction ui.Horizontal (left to right, the default) or ui.Vertical (top to bottom) Width , Height How big it is: see the table below Padding Space inside its edges: ui.Pad(all) , ui.PadXY(horizontal, vertical) Gap Space between its children AlignX , AlignY ui.Start , ui.Center or ui.End : where children sit when there is room to spare Columns Above 0, a grid of that many equal columns Wrap Children that pass the right edge go on to a new line, like words Size Means ui.Fit() As big as its content: the default ui.Grow() Its content plus a share of the space left; GrowBy(2) takes twice the share ui.Share(weight) A share of the space left, starting from nothing (equal shares come out equal: table columns) ui.Fixed(pixels) Exactly that many layout pixels ui.Percent(0.3) A share of the parent ….Between(minimum, maximum) Bounds any of them Sizes are worked out once the whole frame is described, at the end of the frame: a box can grow into space that depends on boxes described after it. When the window is too narrow, growing boxes shrink first, so fixed and fitted ones keep their size. The skeleton The window is a vertical box that fills it: the toolbar, then a horizontal box that grows to take the height left (the list and the content), then the status bar. // build describes the whole interface, in every frame. func (program *register) build(context *ui.Context) { context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { program.toolbar(context) context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { program.sideList(context) program.details(context) }) program.statusBar(context) }) program.confirmRemoval(context) } Painting a box: Frame Box only arranges. Frame also paints, with a ui.Look : a fill, a border, rounded corners, a shadow, a clip. Colours come from the theme , so the dark theme follows on its own: // statusBar sums the register up at the foot of the window. func (program *register) statusBar(context *ui.Context) { lit := 0 for _, light := range program.lighthouses { if light.lit { lit++ } } context.Separator() context.Frame(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.PadXY(16, 6)}, ui.Look{Fill: context.Theme.Surface}, func() { context.Caption(fmt.Sprintf("%d lighthouses, %d lit", len(program.lighthouses), lit)) }) } Separator() draws a thin line across its box. Spacer() takes all the free space of its row or column, pushing what follows to the far end: the toolbar puts one between its title and its search box. // toolbar is the bar across the top: the title, a search box and a menu to add a lighthouse. func (program *register) toolbar(context *ui.Context) { theme := context.Theme bar := ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.PadXY(16, 8), Gap: 8, AlignY: ui.Center} context.Frame(bar, ui.Look{Fill: theme.Surface}, func() { context.Icon("lighthouse") context.Heading("Lighthouses") context.Spacer() // the search box and the Add menu come in lessons 3 and 4 }) context.Separator() } A column you can resize Resizable is a box with a handle on one side. Dragging it writes the new width into your variable, between a minimum and a maximum; the program keeps the variable (and could save it). // sideList lists the lighthouses; lesson 3 makes the rows selectable. func (program *register) sideList(context *ui.Context) { column := ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Height: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(8), Gap: 2} context.Resizable("side", ui.RightSide, &program.sideWidth, 180, 400, column, func() { for _, light := range program.lighthouses { context.Label(light.name) } }) } And the content, for now a hint: func (program *register) details(context *ui.Context) { area := ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(24), Gap: 12} context.Box(area, func() { context.Caption("Choose a lighthouse on the left, or add one.") }) } func (program *register) confirmRemoval(context *ui.Context) {} // lesson 4 Run it and make the window narrow: the content shrinks, the list keeps its width, and the window stops at MinWidth . Shortcuts Call Is Row(content) A full-width horizontal box with the theme's gap, its children centred vertically Column(content) A full-width vertical box with the theme's gap Grid(columns, content) Rows of equal cells Spacer() , Separator() Free space; a thin line Checkpoint A toolbar on top, the list on the left (drag its edge to widen it), a hint in the middle and the status bar at the foot; make the window narrow and the list keeps its width. Achievement unlocked: Surveyor What you learnt Boxes nest; a Layout gives a direction, sizes, padding, gaps and alignment. Fit , Grow , Share , Fixed , Percent : sizes are worked out at the end of the frame. Frame paints a box with a Look , in the theme's colours; Resizable lets the person size it. Bonus (optional) Put the status bar's count on the left and the word "Saved" on the right of the same bar. ← Lesson 1 · Lesson 3: controls and forms →

the-quest/menus-sheets-and-notes.title: Lesson 4: menus, sheets and notes
the-quest/menus-sheets-and-notes.text: Lesson 4: menus, sheets and notes A register needs to grow and shrink. In this lesson you add lighthouses from a menu , ask before removing one with a sheet , and confirm it with a short note (a toast). Mission Pieces Time Adding and removing lighthouses MenuButton , Sheet , Toast 15 min The idea A sheet is a clerk who asks before stamping : while it is open, nothing else on the desk can be touched. It stays exactly as long as your program says (an if ), and tells you when the person waves it away. A menu MenuButton(icon, label, content) is a flat button that opens a menu under it. Its content is described only while it is open; MenuItem returns true when chosen, and choosing closes it. Arrows and Enter work, and Escape or a click elsewhere closes it. It goes at the end of the toolbar, after the search box: context.MenuButton("plus", "Add", func() { if context.MenuItem("lighthouse", "Lighthouse", "") { program.add() } if context.MenuItem("copy", "Copy of the selected one", "") && program.selected >= 0 { program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses, program.lighthouses[program.selected]) program.selected = len(program.lighthouses) - 1 } }) The third argument of MenuItem is a hint drawn quietly on the right, such as "Ctrl+N" : the program handles the shortcut itself ( state.Pressed ), Go UI only shows it. func (program *register) add() { program.added++ program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses, lighthouse{name: fmt.Sprintf("New lighthouse %d", program.added), rangeNM: 10, period: 5}) program.selected = len(program.lighthouses) - 1 program.search = "" } A sheet that asks first A sheet is a modal card in the middle of the window. Like everything else it is shown with an if , for as long as your program wants: here, while program.removing is true. It dims what is behind it and takes the mouse and the keyboard, so nothing behind reacts. // confirmRemoval asks before a lighthouse is taken out of the register. func (program *register) confirmRemoval(context *ui.Context) { if !program.removing { return } name := program.lighthouses[program.selected].name dismissed := context.Sheet("Remove lighthouse", ui.SheetOptions{}, func() { context.Label(fmt.Sprintf("Take %s out of the register?", name)) context.Row(func() { context.Spacer() if context.Button("Keep it") { program.removing = false } if context.PrimaryButton("Remove") { program.remove() context.Toast(name+" was removed", false) } }) }) if dismissed { program.removing = false } } func (program *register) remove() { program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses[:program.selected], program.lighthouses[program.selected+1:]...) program.selected = min(program.selected, len(program.lighthouses)-1) program.removing = false } Sheet returns true on the frame the person asks to close it some other way: Escape, the × in its title, or a click on the dimmed backdrop. Your program decides what that means; here, the same as "Keep it". confirmRemoval is called after the rest of the window in build , so the sheet is described last and drawn over it. The sheet asking before East Cape is removed, the window dimmed behind it A note that goes away Toast(text, warning) shows a short note at the bottom of the window for a few seconds. Unlike everything else it is fired once , not described at every frame: Go UI keeps it until it fades. More layers Call Shows Sheet(title, options, content) A modal card with a title and a ×; returns true when dismissed Modal(name, LayerOptions{…}, content) Your own content over everything, dimming what is behind (a dialog, a drawer) Overlay(name, LayerOptions{…}, content) Your own content over everything, without dimming (a note, a floating button) Popover(name, &open, look, content) A box floating under the control before it (a dropdown of your own) Tooltip(text) A dark note explaining the control before it, after the pointer rests on it Toast(text, warning) A short note at the bottom, fired once LayerOptions.Leave makes a modal or an overlay leave with motion once you stop showing it. Checkpoint Add opens a menu that adds a lighthouse; Remove dims the window under a sheet that asks first; Remove in it takes the lighthouse out and a note says so. Achievement unlocked: Harbourmaster What you learnt A menu's content is described only while open; MenuItem returns true when chosen. A sheet is shown with an if , and returns true when the person dismisses it. What is described later is drawn on top; toasts are fired once. Bonus (optional) Give the Remove button a tooltip, "Takes it out of the register, after asking", and show the "Copy of the selected one" item only when a lighthouse is selected. ← Lesson 3 · Lesson 5: controls of your own →

the-quest/over-a-3d-scene.title: Lesson 6: over a 3D scene

sections.text: With a window of Go UI's

the-quest/over-a-3d-scene.text: Lesson 6: over a 3D scene Go UI was made to draw interfaces over Go Renderer 's scenes. In this lesson you put a panel over an island that moves the sun and the clouds, and learn how the interface and the camera share the mouse. Mission Pieces Time A panel that moves the sun over an island viewer.Run , claims, Options.Scene 15 min The idea The interface and the camera share one mouse, like two people and one remote control : whoever the pointer is over has it. When it is over a panel, Go UI claims it, and the camera gets only what was left. A panel with three sliders over the sample island There are two ways in: viewer.Run (Go Renderer) window.Options.Scene (Go UI) The cameras The viewer's: orbit, walking, map, its keys and flags Yours: a camera.Orbit or anything that fills a camera.Lens Runs on The desktop The desktop, a web page and Android Good for Tools over a scene: editors, inspectors, simulations Applications with a scene inside: a phone app with a map With the viewer The viewer calls your update function at every step; Go UI's frame goes inside it, between Begin and End . You make the context yourself with ui.New() , and hand its drawing to the scene's overlay once: // An interface over a go-renderer scene: a panel that moves the sun and the clouds over the sample // island. package main import ( "flag" "fmt" "log" "math" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/graphics" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/input" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/scene" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/scene/sample" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/viewer" ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" ) func main() { options := viewer.DefaultOptions() options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) flag.Parse() context, err := ui.New() if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } world := sample.Island() world.Overlay.Drawing = context.Drawing() // go-renderer paints what go-ui lays out elevation, azimuth := float32(35), float32(220) // degrees clouds := world.Environment.EffectiveSky().Clouds.Coverage update := func(world *scene.Scene, state *input.State, step float64) { context.Begin(state) context.PanelWith("Sky", ui.PanelOptions{X: 16, Y: 16, Width: ui.Fixed(260)}, func() { context.Label("Sun height") context.Slider("elevation", &elevation, -20, 90) context.Label("Sun bearing") context.Slider("azimuth", &azimuth, 0, 360) context.Label("Clouds") context.Slider("clouds", &clouds, 0, 1) context.Separator() context.Row(func() { context.Caption(fmt.Sprintf("%.0f° up, %.0f° from north", elevation, azimuth)) context.Spacer() if context.Button("Night") { elevation = -15 } }) }) context.End() // lays out, paints, and claims the mouse when it is over the panel world.Environment.SunDirection = sunDirection(elevation, azimuth) world.Environment.EffectiveSky().Clouds.Coverage = clouds } if err := viewer.Run(world, options, "Sky", update); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // sunDirection points towards a sun at an elevation and an azimuth (clockwise from north, −z), in // degrees. func sunDirection(elevation, azimuth float32) graphics.Vector { up := float64(elevation) * math.Pi / 180 around := float64(azimuth) * math.Pi / 180 return graphics.Vector{ float32(math.Cos(up) * math.Sin(around)), float32(math.Sin(up)), float32(-math.Cos(up) * math.Cos(around)), 0, } } go run . # needs go-renderer's scene/sample: no files go run . -walk -dark # every viewer flag works PanelWith is a floating card with a title bar: drag the bar to move it, the chevron folds it. PanelOptions places it ( X , Y ), sizes it, locks it, or docks it to an edge ( Dock: ui.DockLeft ). Who gets the mouse Dragging a slider must not turn the camera. At End , when the pointer is over a panel or a control is held, Go UI claims the mouse for that step ( state.ClaimMouse() ); while a field has the keyboard, it claims the keyboard. The viewer then gives its cameras and shortcuts state.Unclaimed() , a copy without what was claimed. A press that starts on the open scene belongs to the camera until it is let go, even if it passes over a panel. In your own code, context.WantsMouse() and context.WantsKeyboard() say the same, for shortcuts of your own. With a window of Go UI's window.Options.Scene puts a scene behind the interface. It is called at every step after the interface, with the input the interface did not claim, and returns what to show: package main import ( "flag" "log" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/camera" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/graphics" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/input" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/scene/sample" ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" "github.com/akrck02/go-ui/window" ) func main() { options := window.Options{Title: "Island"} options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) flag.Parse() world := sample.Island() minimum, maximum := world.Bounds() middle := graphics.Vector{(minimum[0] + maximum[0]) / 2, 0, (minimum[2] + maximum[2]) / 2, 1} orbit := camera.NewOrbit(middle, maximum[0]-minimum[0]) view := camera.Lens{Up: graphics.Vector{0, 1, 0, 0}} options.Scene = func(state *input.State, step float64) *window.SceneView { orbit.Update(state, step, &view) // state holds only what the interface did not claim return &window.SceneView{World: world, Camera: view} } err := window.Run(options, func(context *ui.Context) { context.PanelWith("Island", ui.PanelOptions{X: 16, Y: 16}, func() { context.Label("Drag the island to turn it.") }) }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } The same island behind a panel, through Go UI's window Boxes painted with a fill take the mouse like panels; a growing box left transparent lets the scene show through, with the camera working inside it. cmd/scene-app lays a whole application around a 3D view this way. Editing what you see Go Renderer's viewer.Edit gives your function a viewer.View , which turns the pointer into a point on the ground ( Go Renderer's tutorial, lesson 5 ). With Go UI in it you get both: panels to choose what to place, the map to place it on. cmd/plan-editor places huts on an island that way, and DragSource with context.DroppedOnScreen() drops a value of yours from a panel onto the scene ( the guide ). Checkpoint Over the sample island, a Sky panel: dragging its sliders moves the sun and the clouds without turning the camera; dragging the island turns it. Achievement unlocked: Lookout What you learnt Over the viewer: ui.New() , Overlay.Drawing = context.Drawing() , and Begin … End in the update function. Over Go UI's window: Options.Scene returns a scene and a camera, on every platform. Go UI claims the mouse and the keyboard it uses, so cameras get only the rest. Bonus (optional) Add a label to the panel that says whether the mouse is over it, from the context. ← Lesson 5 · Lesson 7: shipping it →

the-quest/shipping-it.title: Lesson 7: shipping it
the-quest/shipping-it.text: Lesson 7: shipping it The register works on your computer. In this last lesson it remembers what it was showing, behaves well when it leaves the screen, and runs in a web page and on a phone, from the same code . Mission Pieces Time The register in a browser and on a phone preferences, Hidden , GOOS=js , go-ui-apk 15 min The idea One program, three harbours : the same code sails to a window, a web page and a phone; the window package is the pilot that knows each port. Before leaving one, write down where you were (the preferences), because the phone may close the app without asking. Remembering between runs window.KeepPreference(name, value) keeps a short text under a name: in the user's configuration folder on the desktop, in the page's local storage in a browser, in the application's files on Android. It is written at once. window.Preference(name) reads it back. // keep writes down what should survive the program: the lighthouse chosen and the list's width. func (program *register) keep() { window.KeepPreference("selected", strconv.Itoa(program.selected)) window.KeepPreference("side width", strconv.Itoa(int(program.sideWidth))) } // restore takes up where the last run was left. func (program *register) restore() { if text, found := window.Preference("selected"); found { if selected, err := strconv.Atoi(text); err == nil && selected < len(program.lighthouses) { program.selected = selected } } if text, found := window.Preference("side width"); found { if width, err := strconv.Atoi(text); err == nil { program.sideWidth = float32(width) } } } For a register of real size, keep the data itself in a file of your own (JSON, a database): preferences are for a handful of settings. Leaving the screen On a phone, another application can come up at any moment, and the system may then end yours without a word. Options.Hidden is called when the program leaves the screen (on the desktop, when the window closes; in a browser, when the page is hidden), and Options.Shown when it comes back: program.restore() options.Hidden = program.keep if err := window.Run(options, program.build); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } Waking from another goroutine The window sleeps until something happens. If your data changes elsewhere (a download, a timer), change it so the next frame sees it, then call window.Wake() so there is a next frame. Changing data from two goroutines at once is still a race: hand the result over through a channel, or a mutex the frame also takes. In a web page Built for WebAssembly, window.Run opens the page's canvas instead of a window and draws through WebGL2. Nothing in the program changes: mkdir -p web GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build -o web/register.wasm . cp "$(go env GOROOT)/lib/wasm/wasm_exec.js" web/ cp "$(go list -m -f '{{.Dir}}' github.com/akrck02/go-ui)/web/index.html" web/ # Go UI's page chmod u+w web/index.html # files in the module cache are read-only python3 -m http.server -d web 8080 # then open http://localhost:8080/?program=register Go UI's web/index.html runs name.wasm from ?program=name . The canvas follows the page's size; the clipboard, the keyboard and preferences are the browser's ( in a web browser ). On a phone Built for Android, the same program is the application's activity, drawn through OpenGL ES. A finger is the pointer, so every control works by touch, and the on-screen keyboard comes up for text fields. To package it, use go-ui-apk from Go UI for Android , which needs the Android SDK, the NDK and a JDK, and no Java code, Gradle or Android Studio: go run github.com/akrck02/go-ui-android/cmd/go-ui-apk -name Register -id io.example.register . adb install register.apk A desktop layout is not a phone layout, though: the register's side list and form want a screen each on a phone, with a navigation bar. Go UI for Android's material package draws pieces as Android's own applications do (top bars, navigation bars, lists, sheets), and its tutorial starts where this one ends. On a phone, also look at context.Insets() (the system's bars), context.Size() (to choose a layout by the screen) and context.Back() (the back gesture) ( on Android ). Checkpoint Close and open the register: the same lighthouse is chosen and the list as wide as you left it. Built for WebAssembly, it runs at localhost:8080/?program=register . Achievement unlocked: Shipwright What you learnt KeepPreference and Preference keep settings on every platform; Options.Hidden is the moment to keep them. window.Wake() asks for a frame from another goroutine. The same program runs in a page ( GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm ) and on Android (go-ui-apk). Final challenge · Register keeper Give the register a Settings sheet, opened from a gear button in the toolbar, with a Dark theme toggle. The choice is kept between runs. Hint: a bool in the program, a Sheet shown while it is open, ui.DarkTheme() and ui.LightTheme() , and KeepPreference / Preference for the choice. Try it on your own first, then compare with the solution. The final challenge: the Settings sheet over the register, in the dark theme Rare achievement unlocked: Register keeper Well done Every achievement of the quest Where next The guide : everything about layout, text fields, tables, drag and drop, screen readers, how a frame is drawn. the-quest/the-quest.title: Tutorial: a register of lighthouses
the-quest/the-quest.text: Tutorial: a register of lighthouses The quest map: Switchman, Surveyor, Clerk, Harbourmaster, Craftsman, Lookout, Shipwright, then the final challenge, Register keeper In seven lessons you build a real desktop application, one step at a time: a register of lighthouses with a list to choose one, a form to edit it, a search, a menu, a sheet that asks before removing, and a control of your own. Then you put an interface over a 3D scene, and take the program to a web page and a phone. The finished register: a toolbar with a search box, a list of lighthouses on the left and the form of the one chosen Before you start , follow Get started . Each lesson takes ten to twenty minutes and ends with something you can run. Every lesson has the same shape, as in a quest: the idea in everyday words, the code , a checkpoint to know it works, a bonus with its solution folded, and an achievement to unlock. A final challenge waits at the end of lesson 7. Lesson You learn You end with 1. Immediate mode A frame, controls that return what happened, ids and scopes A lamp to switch on and off 2. Layout Boxes, directions, Fit , Grow , Fixed , padding, gaps, frames The window's skeleton: toolbar, side list, content, status bar 3. Controls and forms Selectable rows, text and number fields, selects, sliders, toggles A form that edits the lighthouse chosen 4. Menus, sheets and notes Menus, modal sheets, toasts, the search Adding and removing lighthouses 5. Controls of your own Clickable , looks, Describe for screen readers, Paint , themes A favourite star, and a theme of your own 6. Over a 3D scene Go UI with Go Renderer's viewer, claims, Options.Scene A panel that moves the sun over an island 7. Shipping it Preferences, leaving the screen, the web, Android The register in a browser and on a phone Lessons end with practice , with a solution folded under it.
